A Real-Time Strategy

Cosy Empires

You lead the Sunfolk against the Ashkin.
Difficulty: Medium

Build 16 August 2026

Choose your match
You have a saved village. Starting a new game will write over it at the next dawn.

You start with one villager and a town centre in ruins.

  • Tap your villager, then tap Gather and tap a tree — or double-tap them and after that every tap just does whatever makes sense where you tapped
  • Bring back wood until there is enough to repair the town centre
  • Then build it out, however you like, into a cosy empire

Something new happens every day. Get everyone indoors at night — there are things out in the dark. And each season brings its own.

Settings

Difficulty is set when you start a game, and can be changed at any time from the ☰ menu, top left — it starts a fresh map.

Sound and a few other things will live here once they exist.

Patch notes
Patch 21.22
In Peaceful, the Ashkin keep pace with you
  • They match the village you are building. Raise a barracks and a barracks goes up across the valley. Take an upgrade and they take the same one. They already caught up to your age this way; now it is what you have actually built, so a long Peaceful game has somebody growing alongside you rather than a neighbour who quietly falls behind and stops mattering
  • They catch up. They never race ahead. They only ever copy something you have got — never reach for something you have not. A rival who keeps pace makes the valley feel alive; one who overtakes you turns Peaceful into a race, which is the one thing it is not
  • And it is the shape, not the layout. What kinds of building, and how far up each ladder — never where you put them. They lay their own village out in their own way; it simply ends up as capable as yours. One thing at a time, on a slow clock, so it reads as a village working rather than buildings appearing the instant yours are finished. They will always be a little behind
  • Never the army, and never a fortress. Peaceful promises they do not come for you, and there is a treaty saying so. A barracks is a building and it is fair game; soldiers are not, and training stays where it was — behind the peace actually being broken. Walls and towers are left out for the same reason: a mirrored fortress reads as a threat whatever the treaty says
Elsewhere
  • The farm panel names what is growing in it — corn, cabbages, strawberries and the rest — instead of only telling you how much was left of something unnamed
  • The army holds its ground. A soldier used to go to bed over a single lost hit point; they now stay out whatever the hour until they are down to a fifth of their health, and may then break off mid-battle for their own barracks and be patched up there at any time of day
  • A rival clan could stall for an entire match and never raise an army. Once they decided to put a barracks up they began saving wood for it — and, while saving, refused to build a woodcutter’s camp, because a camp costs wood. So a clan that reached that decision before it happened to have a camp standing was holding out for wood it had no way of earning: it sat on a growing pile of food, never quite reached the price of the barracks, and fielded nobody at all. Woodcutters’ camps now go up regardless, since a camp is the one thing that pays the saving back. The trap had been there all along and was only ever avoided by luck — the clans that escaped it were the ones that happened to build a camp first
  • The town centre’s first upgrade is priced for the age it belongs to. The hens kept the cost they had when they were a separate purchase much later on — which asked for a good deal of knowledge, a thing you have almost none of that early. It now asks for timber, stone and feed, in line with every other first rung in the game
Three trades are earned by doing the work
  • Nobody finds a gardener in the woods any more. Three of the finds are gone — the cuttings, the odd heavy stone and the old tool. Those trades have an ordinary job behind them, so they go to whoever has actually been doing it, three days at a stretch: days among the trees make a Gardener, days in the fields make a Caretaker, days at the rock face makes a Geologist. One job each, so no two of them are ever chasing the same villager’s work
  • And somebody who has earned a trade is somebody everywhere. They walk about under a name and a title from the moment they earn it — Saga the Caretaker — so the panel calls them by it instead of “Villager”, they wear the trade’s own colours, and putting them in a group no longer drags every villager in the place in behind them. The caretaker also keeps the clothes they were wearing when their cottage goes up, rather than turning into a stranger the moment they move in
  • The moonlit mushroom belongs to the whole village, not to whoever picked it up. It is the one find the founder may fetch — they carry the only torch after dark, so they are the one out where a thing that glows in the dark is found — and it costs them nothing, because it is whoever raises the hut who becomes the herbalist. Any villager but the founder can be the one to do that
  • They are still yours until the cottage stands. They take the name, the title and the clothes straight away, and go on being an ordinary villager you can order anywhere — the title does not lapse if you send them off to chop wood. Raising their cottage is their own button, and finishing it is the moment they become the specialist and leave your hands for good
  • And it is the one who earned it who takes it, not whoever happens to lay the last plank — with a build crew that is very often somebody else who came over to help
  • The founder is never eligible, for these as for everything else. It is a village of other people
Spotted, and put right
  • The northern lights are put away for now. Not removed — everything that draws them and lights the ground beneath them is still there and still right, and they can come back exactly as they were whenever you want them. Only the roll that starts one is refused
  • Two odd little tabs on the bottom corners of the hall’s roof. Its first two ages draw a tall triangle of their own, and that triangle stood three pixels proud of the wall either side — an ordinary eave, and on an ordinary shallow roof it reads as one. This pitch is very nearly vertical where it meets the wall, so a flat little spur at the bottom of it did not read as an overhang at all. The triangle sits on its walls now, and is simply a triangle
  • The whole village kept ending up in the fisherman’s group. A group remembers the kinds of unit in it, so anything you train later of the same kind falls straight in — which is right for eight spearmen and quite wrong for the fisherman, because a fisherman is a villager. Putting him in a group claimed every villager in the game for it, and every one raised afterwards was swept in behind him. The same fault meant two trades could never hold a group each: grouping the bug catcher tore the claim back off the fisherman’s group. The people who are somebody in particular — the founder and the trades — can sit in a group now without lending their kind to it
  • The granary’s man never went to bed. Everyone else with a building of their own turns in at dusk; he had simply never been given the rule, and was still out at midnight pottering about the yard a few steps from his own door. He walks back and goes in now, and comes out again in the morning
  • Villagers were walking about underneath the fields. A field is ground you walk over — that has always been true — so it is drawn behind everyone standing on it. When the crops grew tall enough to be worth looking at, fields were moved into the ordinary depth order so a berry bush behind one would stop covering the corn; and that put the soil itself over anybody working at the field’s top edge. Both wants are real, so a field is drawn in two parts now: the soil and the far fence at the very back where they belong, and the tall crop standing in the world in its own right. A bush behind the field goes down first, a villager on the field walks in front of it, and one standing among the corn is partly hidden by the rows nearer you
  • The bees were hidden almost all year. Bees and butterflies fade in with the blossom — but blossom only ever happens in spring, so every bee in the game was skipped outright for the other three seasons. Six of the eight kinds are all-year or autumn creatures, and the Ivy Bee, whose own note in the book reads “the very last bee of the year, and it works until the frost”, had never once been drawn. Spring still brings them out with the flowers; the rest of the year they are simply about
  • The panel for whoever you have selected was squashed. It is a column about a hundred pixels wide — narrower still when a building’s description sits beside it — and it was being handed six lines at once: name, type, health, attack, what they were carrying, how long they had been about and every deed they had earned, all in the same small grey text. It now answers the question you clicked them to ask, in three lines: who they are, what they are — Founder, Fisherman, Bug catcher, Spearman — and what they are doing right now. Everything with a number on it moved below, where it scrolls
  • The health figure is gone from the top of that panel. Anyone hurt already carries a bar over their head, so the number was spending a line of a very narrow column repeating something the world was showing anyway. It is still there among the stats
  • All the hens ended up in one heap. Two faults on top of each other. The walk towards somebody carrying a full basket aimed every bird at very nearly the same point — and re-aimed her there sixty times a second, so they converged and then jittered in the pile. And there was no rule anywhere keeping hens out of each other’s way, so any shared attraction stacked the yard: a full basket, the door in a downpour, a farm they all set off to visit. Measured with five hens and somebody stood still holding food, the closest two went from twelve pixels apart to less than half a pixel, with every pair in the yard inside six. Each hen keeps her own side of the basket now, fixed when she hatches, and hens standing about make room for one another
  • The seasonal drifts can be caught now. Spring’s bloomtide beetles and summer’s dragonflies have drifted over the fields for a long time in a system of their own that the bug book knew nothing about — you could watch them and nothing happened when you tapped one. They are proper species now: summer’s jewel colours turn out to be the damselflies and chasers the book already had, and and spring’s pastel bloomtide beetles go in as May Bugs, the spring beetle it already had. The book stays at 101. Autumn’s gossamer and winter’s diamond dust stay uncatchable on purpose — one is spider silk and the other is ice
  • Villagers kneel to pick berries instead of gathering from a bush bolt upright with one arm out. One knee down, the other up, and they lower themselves into it and get up again rather than snapping. A farm’s own crop is still worked standing
  • The yellow box round a selected building went over the top of it — straight across the front of the roof. Units, the elder and the beasts have drawn their selection ring from underneath themselves for a long time, precisely so it would not sit painted over them; buildings had simply been left out of it. A building stands in its box now
  • No more glow on the magnifying glass at dusk. That light is there because the other trade finds are things you go out into the dark and hunt — a glitter in the treeline, something flowering past the last field. The starting glass lies two tiles from your hall and a line tells you it is there, so the glow was doing no work
  • The northern lights fill the sky. They were three ribbons across the top hundred pixels and nothing below — on a tall screen it read as a decorated border. Nine bands over the whole view now, each with its own drift and thickness, fading down towards the ground so it still reads as something happening far overhead. It is one of the rarest sights in the game and it was easy to miss entirely
The other eight crops
  • Seven of the nine crops were the same picture in different greens. Cabbage, kale, turnip, carrot, strawberry, pumpkin and sweet potato all came out of the same three lines — one flat oval a plant, plus a coloured dot if the crop had fruit. Two of them have no fruit at all, so they were not merely similar, they were identical. Come in close and each is itself now: a cabbage is a tight ball of leaves wrapped round a pale heart; kale is loose and very frilly with no ball at all; a turnip and a carrot show the shoulder of the root above the soil, one with broad tops and one with fine feathery ones; strawberries have three leaflets to a leaf and pips on the fruit; a pumpkin is a ribbed gourd with a stalk and a vine leaf behind it; the sweet potato trails a vine of heart-shaped leaves
  • Pea pods have peas in them, and the tendril that holds the vine up — which is what you recognise a row of peas by
  • Three crops could barely be seen at all. Kale and the sweet potato are pure foliage — no fruit, no ear, no flower — so their leaf colour was the only thing between them and the earth, and it was not enough: a field of either was very nearly an empty field, at any zoom. The pea pod had the same fault against its own vine, and was darker than the leaves it hung among. All three now stand as far off their background as the cabbage always did
  • None of the close-up work is drawn until you are close enough to make it out, so an ordinary view costs nothing
Bringing a harvest in
  • A field being cut looked like nothing at all. Working it only ever made the crop a little shorter — by at most a third — and left its colour and the number of plants alone. Taking a field of corn from full down to a fifth changed under three per cent of what you could see, less than a single day’s growth, and then it went to bare drills all at once. The half of the cycle you actually cause was the half that did not show
  • A field is taken plant by plant now, from the near edge back, leaving pale stubble on the turned earth behind. What is still standing stands at full height — it has not shrunk, it has not been cut yet — so you can watch the standing crop retreat towards the far fence as the crew work through it. Near edge first on purpose: cut from the back and the crop still standing hides its own stubble, which looks like nothing again
  • The cut line is ragged rather than row by row, so a field does not blink out a whole row at a time
  • This is every crop, not just the ones with a close-up — corn, sunflowers, wheat, and the six still to come
Wheat
  • An ear of wheat was a single bead on the end of a stick, in a colour so close to the straw it grew on that it read as the stalk being slightly fatter at the tip. An ear is a spike: grains in two staggered ranks, and the long bristles — awns — going up off the top, which are what you actually recognise a wheat field by. It has both now, and the ear nods as it fills, because a ripe one is heavy
  • The grain fills from the base of the ear upwards, so a field just come into ear is not a field ready to cut. Before this, a field on day two and the same field in full ear were very nearly the same picture
  • The ears also read from an ordinary distance now, not only close up: they stand nearly twice as far off the straw in colour as they did, which is about where the corn’s cobs sit
Sunflowers, and what was standing in front of them
  • A sunflower was a yellow disc with a brown dot in it — a bullseye on a green pole. Close in it now has a ring of petals, a seeded centre that only darkens once there is seed to show, green sepals behind, and the broad drooping leaves that are most of what makes a sunflower a sunflower. A ripe head nods, because one full of seed is too heavy to hold itself up
  • The flower was not attached to its own stem. The stalk leaned in the wind and breathed a little in height — and the head did neither, because it was placed from its own arithmetic rather than the stalk’s. So in any breeze a sunflower head sat beside its stalk and drifted against it, on both axes, by as much as four pixels on a head three across. Reported exactly that way. Head and stalk take their lean and their height from one place now, so they cannot disagree. The same fault had wheat’s ears and the pea pods off their stems too
  • A field was drawn behind everything on the map. Right while a field was flat green rows on the ground; wrong the day the crops grew tall, because a berry bush standing well behind a field was still painted over the top of the sunflowers in front of it. Fields take their place in the world like anything else now — what is behind them goes down first, what is in front comes after, and the workers on them stay visible
A field goes on living after it ripens
  • Four of a crop’s seven days were the same picture. A field reached full ear on day three and then stood pixel for pixel identical until somebody cut it or the season turned. The growth clock simply stopped. It runs on now, and what it tracks after ripeness is how long the crop has been standing there
  • A pumpkin patch left standing gets barer, not busier. The vine dies back: the big leaves yellow, shrivel and go, and the gourds are left sitting out on open ground, which is the whole picture of a patch in late autumn. The fruit goes on curing meanwhile — a light orange deepening to a deep red-orange — and the stalk hardens off woody and grey
  • The sweet potato cracks the ground open. It is the one crop whose crop is out of sight, so it had nothing to show for the days after it was ready. The tell is the ground itself: a tuber that goes on swelling heaves the earth until the soil splits above it, in fine fissures running out from the crown, and that is exactly what a grower looks for. It is a winter crop besides, so the vine bronzes and the leaves droop as the cold gets into them
  • A strawberry bed left standing runs. Long bare stems reach out sideways from each crown and set a daughter plant down at the tip, so the bed sprawls out of its rows instead of sitting neatly in them — and any fruit still hanging goes from bright red to a dull deep crimson, slumped a little wider and lower, with the pale pips fading into it. Four days of a strawberry bed being left alone, and none of it was drawn
  • Carrot tops stand tall. They are ferny things that go well above the row, and they were drawn at the same squat height as a turnip’s — so a carrot bed read as a turnip bed with finer leaves. They are nearly four times taller at full growth now, taller than the peas and far above every other low crop, and the height comes on with the plant: barely up the day they are sown, towering by the time they are ready
  • A carrot left in the ground greens at the crown. Its shoulder edges up out of the soil as it swells, and the part that has been out in the light makes chlorophyll — that green top is the mark of one that has been in the ground a while. The feathery tops darken with it. A turnip beside it does the opposite: it shoulders much further clear, and goes yellow rather than green
  • Turnips heave out of the ground. A root goes on swelling after it is ready, and a swelling root lifts its own shoulder clear of the soil — which is the very thing you look for to know one is ready to pull. The tops coarsen, yellow and flop out over it as the days go by
  • Kale goes lollipop. Kale is shed from the bottom up — the outer leaves go, the crown keeps putting up new ones — so a plant left standing ends as a tuft of leaves riding a bared stem, which is exactly what an old kale looks like. And the cold turns what is left toward purple, which is what kale does and what makes it a winter crop worth having
  • A cabbage left in the ground bolts. It used to sit there being a cabbage from the day it headed until somebody cut it. Now the outer leaves loosen and splay, and yellow from the edge inwards while the heart — wrapped up inside — keeps its colour longest. Leave it past about day five and it bolts: a flower stalk pushes straight up out of the middle, which is exactly what a crop left too long looks like
  • Peas dry on the vine. A pod stopped changing the moment it had its peas in it. One left standing dries instead: it shrinks onto the peas so they show harder rather than softer, the pod goes from bright green to a pale parchment, and the vine and its tendrils yellow off and curl tighter. A row that has stood a few days looks ready to pick
  • Wheat dries in the field. An ear stopped bending the moment it filled. Grain goes on drying after that, and the neck goes on bending with it — so from day three the ears hang further and further over, the straw bleaches from a live gold to the pale dry colour of a field waiting to be cut, and the awns splay out and bristle. A week-old field looks ready in a way a three-day-old one does not
  • Sunflowers go to seed. A head kept exactly the pose it struck the day it opened. The weight of seed keeps arriving after the petals are out, so from day three on it nods further and further over, sheds its petals one at a time until only a ragged few are left, and the middle darkens and fills. By the end of the season it is a seed head looking at the ground rather than a flower looking at you
  • Corn dries where it stands. A cob does not keep growing once it is made — what happens is that the plant around it goes off. From day three to day seven the leaves and husks turn from green to straw, the stalks pale with them, and the cob itself deepens from a bright yellow to a dry amber. Every one of those days now looks different from the last
Corn, close up
  • An ear of corn is an ear of corn now. It was a filled rectangle a pixel and a half wide — which is the right drawing from an ordinary view, and nothing at all once you lean right in. Come close and a cob has husk leaves gripping it, a body that swells and turns from pale to gold, and kernels in staggered rows, with silk at the tip once it is ready. The stalks have their long drooping leaves and a tassel on top, which is most of what makes corn read as corn from across a field
  • And the ear fills in as it ripens, from the base upwards — 45 kernels on one that has just set, 195 on one ready to cut. Without that a new cob carried exactly as many kernels as a ripe one and merely got bigger, so being able to see them told you nothing
  • None of it is drawn until you are close enough to resolve a kernel, so an ordinary view pays nothing for it
  • The far side of a field’s fence was standing in front of the crop. Posts and rails were all drawn after whatever was growing, so the back row of stakes and the top rail sat on top of the back row of plants. That was wrong for every crop and unmissable once the corn was tall enough to reach them. A field is a box you look into: the far side goes down first, the near side last
  • Behind it, a colour bug that had been quietly painting things black. The routine that lightens or darkens a colour only ever understood #hex, and half the colours in the game are mixed ones handed over in another form — fed one of those it produced a near-black that threw no error and looked like a deliberate dark outline. So every mixed-then-shaded colour in the game drew black. It had been found twice before and stepped around both times without the routine itself being fixed; one line does the lot. The sunflower’s closed bud, black since the day it was added, is green
The grass knows you are walking through it
  • The bed itself parts now. Walk somebody across a meadow and the grass they are actually standing in leans away from them — opening ahead, closing behind, and easing back upright over a second or so rather than snapping to attention the moment a boot leaves it. It is the grass that was already on the ground doing this, not a few blades worn on the shins: the tiles somebody is standing in stop being stamped and are drawn blade by blade instead, from the same pattern the field is built from, so they are the very blades that were there a moment before
  • Animals move it too. A deer crossing a meadow parts the grass exactly as a villager does, and so do the dogs. Beasts and raiders are left out on purpose — grass reacting in the middle of a fight is detail nobody is looking at
  • And it was a comb before. What used to happen was four blades at fixed spacing, all leaning the same way, the only difference between one villager and the next being one of three possible offsets — which is why it looked identical on everybody, all the time. Blades are now scattered, sized and stiffened individually, so no two people stand in the same grass
  • Grass was growing on the beach, and not on a third of the grass. Every place in the game that asked "does grass grow here?" asked it the same wrong way — and the comment sitting beside the question said what was meant: water, sand, bare dirt. But it named the darker of the three grasses where it meant sand. So one grass tile in three was left bald, and the beaches were sown instead — and since sand sits right on the waterline with the sea drawn over part of it, that is what put grass in the ocean. Grass grows on grass now, and a beach is a beach
  • A blade is a shape now, not a stick. Every blade in the game was a drawn line with a rounded end — the same width at the tip as at the root, with a dome on top. That is a capsule, and at any size it reads as a scatter of little green sticks. It was the real reason the grass never looked right however short it was cut: the height had already come down and it still looked wrong, because the height was never the problem. Blades are proper tapered shapes now, wide where they leave the ground and meeting at a point
  • And the blades at somebody’s boots are the ground’s own. They used to be a separate little bunch invented for each villager — and with the bed itself faint close up, those few were the only grass you could see, so everyone walked about wearing a small green bush. The blades crossing a pair of boots are now simply the ones that happen to grow there, at the angle the ground has them. There is nothing left to look attached
  • And it came down to the knee. A villager is sixteen pixels tall and the tallest blades were fourteen — the grass stood at four-fifths the height of the people walking through it. Nobody noticed while it was a flat texture; the moment blades began bending one at a time they read as separate stalks and the village turned out to be wading through a wheat field
  • Behind all of this: the version of that effect written to make grass part around a walker had never once run. A second function of the same name sat below it in the same file and silently replaced it — so what everybody saw was an older, simpler version leaning only on the wind. There is now a check that refuses to let any two functions share a name, because this cannot be seen at runtime: the feature simply looks worse than the code says it should
No two animals quite the same
  • Every species had exactly one colour. So two deer standing together were the same deer twice, and a herd read as a copy-paste rather than as a herd. Every animal now carries a look of its own, rolled once when it is born and kept for as long as it lives: a coat a little lighter or darker than its kind, a marking, and a build a touch bigger or smaller. Two deer are now the same deer well under one time in a hundred, where before it was every time
  • Six markings, and most animals have none. That is the point — a wood full of piebald deer would be as wrong as a wood full of identical ones, so about half of them are simply plain. The rest carry pale flecks along the back, a darker patch on the flank, a pale muzzle and throat, pale lower legs, or a darker band over the shoulders. It should read as "those two are different" without your ever noticing why
  • And it stays inside what an animal looks like. A coat is a shade of the species' own colour, never a new one. A white animal — a snow fox, an ermine, a winter hare — gets a third of the range and no dark markings at all, because two shades down a snow fox is just a grubby fox. Nothing legless gets pale socks. And the Golden Stag, which the whole village is told about when it appears, is left exactly as it always was
  • The smaller creatures too. Ducks are drakes or ducks now, dark-headed or brown through, instead of one identical bird repeated across the water. Squirrels are red or grey. Hens come in three plumages rather than one. And the birds in a skein vary in size and darkness from one another — they already flapped out of step, but were otherwise the same stamp printed five times
  • Measured on a real map: of a hundred and seventy-four pairs of animals of the same species, three were indistinguishable. It used to be all of them
Put right
  • Whoever picked up the magnifying glass never became the bug catcher. Two faults, one on top of the other. Picking a trade find up gives the finder a follow-on errand to carry it home — and the very next line wiped that errand the same instant it was set, so they simply stood there holding the glass, never walked to the hall, and the village went on telling you nobody had a glass. Reported exactly that way. Underneath it, a second one: if there was no finished town centre to carry it to — which is the ordinary state of the whole Wandering Age, and the glass now lies two tiles from that ruin on the first morning — the find was thrown away outright, and that trade was gone for the rest of the match with nothing said. They keep hold of it now and take it in the moment there is somewhere to take it to
  • The town centre has one upgrade per age, and the first age's is the hens. "Storehouse Doors" is gone. The hens used to be a button of their own on the hall's panel, bought with a flag of their own, sitting right next to the upgrade ladder that already does exactly that job — two ways of buying the same kind of thing from the same building. They are simply the ladder's first rung now: Hens, then the Council Floor, then the Great Keep, one for each age you can be in
  • The queue said "Villagerx2resting until morning". The spaces were in the text all along; the row is a flex layout, and flex throws away whitespace that sits on its own between items. It reads properly now
  • Speech bubbles no longer float beside houses with nobody under them. A villager who has stepped indoors is not drawn, but anything they had to say still was — hanging over the patch of grass where they happened to be standing when they went in. It was never only the sleepers: any message landing on somebody who had just gone inside did the same. And the dreaming is put away for now, out of the night's roster rather than left in it doing nothing, so it does not go on taking nights from the events that do happen
  • The wolf pup does not just sit there any more. It appeared once a year and then stayed in exactly one spot, in exactly one attitude, with no legs at all, until somebody walked out to it. It keeps its own hours now, on the day clock rather than a stopwatch: it wanders in out of the trees, settles, hangs about for the best part of a day, wanders out again, and turns up a couple of days later somewhere else entirely — at any hour, not only after dark. It has legs, and three ways of waiting: sat up with them folded, lying down with its front paws stretched out ahead of it, or standing on all four to see who is coming. The first time it is heard is announced the way it always was; a return gets a quieter line, since by then the village has met it.

    Measured over ten days: three visits, and it walks a good thousand pixels doing it rather than blinking from place to place. And the moment somebody actually sets off for it, it stays exactly where it is — a pup that wandered off from under an approaching villager would make the whole errand unwinnable, and the walk is already the price of it
  • The bug catcher could not deliver a bug. They walked back and forth by the hall for ever, carrying it. They were being sent to a point half a tile below the building's centre — which is still inside the walls of anything bigger than a single tile — so they came up against the side of it and paced at a destination they could never reach. They are sent to the door now, clear of the footprint, and check the ground on the way so a house backed against water still gets somewhere its owner can stand
  • A bug standing on something can be tapped again. Both taps looked for a bug only after everything else had missed. That was fine while the insects were scattered over the map and stopped working the day they were gathered in around the village — a bug on a house or a woodpile could not be reached at all, because the thing behind it always won. Whichever is nearer your finger now wins: land closer to the creature than to the thing behind it and you get the creature. Land on both and the building or the tree still keeps it, which is right — a woodpile is an enormous thing to want and a bug is three pixels across
  • Two small grey corners hung in the air off the top of every pitched roof. The battens across the slope were drawn the full width of the building at every height, while the roof itself narrows towards the ridge, so near the top they ran straight out through the pitch. They are cut to the width of the roof at their own height now
  • The army holds its ground. A soldier who had lost so much as a single hit point went off to bed at dusk — the bar for "wounded" was any damage at all — so an army that had traded one blow emptied itself into the barracks the moment the light went. They now stay exactly where they are, all night, whatever has happened to them, until they are down to a fifth of their health. At that point they may break off and make for their own barracks or range to be patched up, and they can do it mid-battle rather than waiting for evening: the old code only ever looked at the army once, as the light went, so somebody cut to pieces at noon fought on at a fifth of their health until nightfall. Mending pays out at any hour now for the same reason. Only your own fighters — never a villager, never a scout, never somebody already posted
  • The farm says what is growing in it. The panel gave you "Crop: 155 / 240" — how much was left, and nothing at all about what it was — while the field itself has been growing corn or cabbages or strawberries the whole time. It names them now
  • The fox was barely a fox. Reported as an animal that was hard to identify, and it did not survive a close look: its tail was laid over the body so the two merged into one shape, the white tip was a ball the size of its head stuck on the end of that shape, and the face was a thin triangle with no head behind it. It has a proper head, a short muzzle, small sharp ears, an eye and a nose — and a brush held out clear of the body with a small white end. The tail was then found to be detached, floating off the shoulder: it was rotated the wrong way round, so the end meant to meet the body pointed into open air
  • And a weasel is not a rabbit. Only the medium-sized animals ever checked whether they had a brush, so the weasel, marten, otter and polecat were all drawn with a rabbit's body and a pair of long rabbit ears. They get the low fox shape they should have had
  • Gumby and Floyd look like schnauzers now. They were meant to be a pair of them and only had a token nod to it — a small chin smudge and one brow — so at any distance they read as two scruffy terriers. What actually makes a schnauzer recognisable is the face rather than the body: a squared-off muzzle, heavy brows growing out over the eyes, and a beard hanging well below the jaw. All three are now the whole shape of them, along with the pale furnishings down the legs. Gumby is salt-and-pepper and Floyd stays black, so size and colour still tell the two apart at a glance
  • The house night lights are off for now. The warm circles a building laid on the ground read as pale discs lying on the grass rather than as lamplight. Only the painted oval is hidden — a lit building still lifts the darkness around it exactly as before, so nothing you can actually see at night has changed
  • The bug catcher wears a cap. Blue and white, two panels and a peak, no badge on it — so you can tell who has the glass from across the village rather than only when their hands are in view. It replaces the gauze veil, which was the better idea on paper and the worse one on screen: pale, see-through and wider than the head, it read as a smudge at map zoom and disappeared altogether against snow
  • The beetles were walking backwards. All of them, along with the ladybirds and the spiders. A crawling bug travels in the direction it is pointing, but every one of those bodies drew its head at the back — so they have been trundling about the village head last since the day they were added. They lead with their heads now, and a ladybird's spots and wing-case seam sit behind the head where they belong rather than over it
  • The boar had no head. It was a body-shaped oval with a blunt wedge the same colour stuck on the front, which only made the oval lumpier, and a large white triangle for a tusk. From any distance it read as "some animal, and something has gone wrong with it". It has a proper head now — a heavy wedge set a shade darker so it reads apart from the body, an ear, an eye, a dark snout, and a tusk that is a short curve of ivory rather than a slab
  • And a fox's ears were floating above its head. A clear third of a radius of grass between the two. They sit on the skull now, and there are two of them: a single triangle on a pointed face read as a horn
Patch 21.21
Fishing is a thing you do, not a thing you wait for
  • Sending somebody to a shoal used to be gathering with a different picture on it: they stood there and food arrived. There is a whole quiet game in it now, and it is deliberately the slowest thing in the village — something to go and do when you want a break from building, not another job to manage
  • The cast. Tap an angler at the water and they draw the rod back and wait for you. A gauge runs up the right of the screen with a sweet spot on it that will not stay still, and you flick — hard, or long, it will take either — to send the line out. No timer on this half. Nothing is chasing you. Land in the sweet spot and the fish are better before you have caught anything at all
  • Then the reeling in. The familiar bar, but slower than it was and with twenty real speeds behind it rather than a handful, so no two rounds feel quite the same. Stop it in the green and you have your fish. Miss and you have not lost anything except the cast — and the rod comes straight back up out of the water, ready to go again, instead of leaving you to work out whether it is your turn
  • Both sweet spots. A good cast and a good catch is the point of the whole thing: measured, it takes a fish from about half its possible size to over four fifths of it, and roughly doubles the chance of something scarce. It is worth learning, and it is not required
  • Fifty-five things to catch, and they are numbered. Eighteen ordinary fish that will bite anywhere at any hour. Twenty that only come in one season and only in daylight, five to a season, and none of them common. Thirteen that are night fish. Three that live in genuinely deep water and look like it. And a boot — one, unnumbered by any season or hour, and hardly ever
  • The catch card. Every fish you land stops the game and shows itself: drawn, named, weighed, told what kind of thing it is and given a sentence about itself, with its number in the corner so you can see what you are missing. Close it with its x and it asks whether you want to go again. Something scarce arrives with its name running in colour and a scatter of sparkles that fade
  • The book fills up sensibly. A fish you have never caught is weighted to come up more often than one you already have, which is the difference between a collection that finishes and one that leaves you four fish short for ever. Measured against a decent player's pace: everything caught in about fifteen hours of fishing, and everyone gets there eventually rather than a good share of players stalling out permanently
  • The glowing pool. After dark, one pool somewhere on your coast comes up lit. It is the only place several fish exist, it moves with the seasons but stays put within one, and it is gone by dawn
  • A creel that fills. Five fish and the angler takes them home by themselves — to the Fisherman's House if you have built one, or wherever else will take food — and then walks back out to the water and carries on. You do not have to watch them
  • Shoals run out now, and come back. They always had a stock and it was never once spent, because anything empty was swept up before the timer that would have refilled it could be set — so the code that brings a shoal back had never run, not once, in the whole life of the game. Water is kept when it empties and refills a season later. Fishing a spot to nothing and moving on is now a real thing that happens
  • Shoals sit out in the water. They were being placed hard against the shoreline — about a quarter of them looked beached in the sand. Under one in forty now, with the same number of shoals on the map. There are also half as many fish moving in each one; they were packed too tightly to read as anything but a clump
  • There is a magnifying glass out in the trees from the first morning. Every village starts with one lying in the leaf litter a short walk away — nothing announces where, you simply have to send somebody out to look. It used to be locked behind three doors at once: a settled village, an hour of proper darkness, and a twice-a-season roll, which meant a whole match could go by without ever learning the trade existed. A glass on a brass handle in the leaf litter — and whoever carries it home does not put it down again. They take the coat, the jars and the name, and they stay yours: an ordinary villager you can still order about, the way the fisherman is. One collector at a time, and if you lose them the woods offer another glass.

    There is a book of a hundred to go with it, and it works like the catch book: numbered in groups, cards filling in as you take them. Most of them are the bees, butterflies, grasshoppers and dragonflies already flying about your village wearing a hundred different coats — and four of them are the same ordinary bodies in the colour of moonstone. A Moonstone Firefly is a firefly. That is exactly why seeing one matters. Once five kinds are in the book, the catcher can raise a Bug Catcher's House, one to a village, and the book lives on it. Until then they are an ordinary villager in every way that matters — you order them about, they chop wood, they sleep in whatever house has a bed free, and a catch is walked back to the town centre instead. Once the house is up it is theirs: it is where they sleep, and where the jars go.

    The book is in seven parts, and every card you have not filled still tells you where to go looking: the common run, the seasonal ones, after dark, at the water, when it rains, far from any village, and the moonstone four. A card you have taken is drawn in its own colours with its name and how many you have had; one you have not is a grey shape and a question mark. Snails and worms are drawn as snails and worms — the only things in the book with no legs at all, which is the first thing anybody looks for.

    Bugs come and go now, and the book can be finished. Catching one removed it and nothing ever put another out, so the world quietly emptied as you played — and the book asks for a hundred and one catches from a map that only ever held about fifty bugs. Worse, a bug kept whatever kind it was for as long as that kind made sense, so seven beetles on the map could only ever show you seven of the twenty-four beetles in the book. Between them the collection could not be completed at all: measured, seventy-seven kinds of a hundred and one ever appeared in fifty minutes, and sixteen beetles never turned up once.

    The population is held at whatever the map started with. Anything taken is replaced, arrivals turn up where you are not looking rather than popping in under your nose, and one that has drifted well away from everybody is quietly moved on and comes back as something else. Measured after: ninety-six of the hundred and one in the same run, and the handful left are the ones genuinely waiting on a season, on rain, or on the moonstone's own luck.

    Somebody has to be at the water, too. A few kinds only live at the water's edge, and a bug can only be one of them if it is standing there. Dragonflies, mayflies and snails were put by the water on purpose; a water beetle or a pond skater only ever got there by accident of the map, so on a village without much shoreline they were unmeetable. The waterside is stocked deliberately now, and kept stocked.

    Every one of the hundred and one can actually be met. Fifty-nine of them could not. The book draws on twelve different bodies and the world only ever put five of them on the map — a bee, a butterfly, a grasshopper, a dragonfly and a ladybird — and a bug can only be named as something that shares its body. So every beetle, moth, mayfly, firefly, spider, snail and worm in the book was not rare or well hidden, it was absent. There are seven new bodies out there now, each where its own kind actually lives and each moving in its own way: beetles trundle, spiders sit still and then scuttle, snails barely move at all, worms come up in the wet, moths blunder about after dark, fireflies drift and blink, and mayflies hang over the water and bob. And whether something counts as being "at the water" is now read off where it is standing rather than off what shape it is — a mayfly on the bank could never be a water species before, because it was not a dragonfly.

    And the hundred are out there now. The bugs flying about your village used to be three hard-coded kinds that had never heard of the book — so the book could promise you a Frost Glow-Worm while the world had no idea the thing existed. Every bug on the map is now some particular one of the hundred, and which one depends on the hour, the season, the weather and the ground it is standing on. The same sprite is a Gatekeeper through the summer and something else by autumn. Daylight insects no longer fly about at midnight: after dark the bees and the butterflies are simply not there, and the crickets and moths are. Ladybirds have been added as their own creature — the one thing out there that neither darts, hops nor loops, it just walks — and there are two kinds of them.

    #101, the Thunderstorm Beetle. A dull slate thing that comes down close to the village only while it is actually thundering, and is gone with the storm. It does not glow the way a firefly does; it throws a spark — dark, dark, dark, one hard white crack, dark again — and no two of them crackle in time. It is the only entry in the book whose rule is the weather rather than the hour, so it has a part of its own: When it thunders.

    Taking one. See a bug, pick your bug catcher, tap Gather, tap the bug. They walk over and take it — from somewhat near, not from standing on it, because a bug does not wait where you tapped. It goes in the book, named and numbered, and five kinds is still what unlocks the house. The catching game itself comes next; for now the taking is the whole of it.

    They are the Bug Catcher now rather than the Collector, which is what the village was calling them anyway, and a group with them in it shows a ladybird on its number. The clue that starts all of it leads with the noise rather than the glint — the trees going loud with a hundred small voices where there should be none.

    The house has a face at last. It went out as a plain box with a green roof, standing next to a Fisherman's House with a boat bay, netting and an anchor on it. It now has a shelf of glass jars against the front wall, corked, with something in each, and a butterfly net stood up beside the door.

    And the bug catcher looks like one. They were meant to have their glass in hand and a hat of their own from the start; both were written and neither has ever appeared. The whole lot sat one brace inside the fisherman's costume, so it only ever drew on a fisherman — which meant a bug catcher has been an ordinary villager holding a pickaxe for the entire life of the trade. They now carry the magnifying glass in their hand the way the gardener carries a bucket and the fisherman a rod — brass rim, glass you can see the ground through, a glint on it, and a handle long enough that you can plainly see it being held rather than stuck to their fist — and wear a soft moss cap with a brim of pale netting, the same gauze as the net by their door. The glass has been redrawn as well: it was a disc the size of a coin tucked behind their ear, and it read as nothing at all.

    And the catching game. Tap the catcher, tap Gather, tap a bug — and now you have to earn it, over three rounds.

    Two laps of a circle, then a shape. A red dot sets off clockwise round a ring and you keep your finger on it the whole way. It will not move until your finger is on the start, so nobody is caught out by a clock that began without them. The speed is slow, steady or quick — drawn fresh each round, and never the same twice running, so the second lap is the gesture you have just learned at a pace you did not choose. Slow is not the easy one, either: the margin tightens as the pace drops, so a slow lap is a test of patience where a quick one is a test of nerve.

    The last round is an odd shape. Fourteen of them — a tilted oval, a figure of eight, a lazy eight, a bean, a peanut, a three-leaf, a clover, a scalloped ring, a blossom, a wavy ring, a cloud, a loop within a loop, a daisy, and a looped knot that crosses itself so you cannot navigate by the part you have already covered. Every one is a smooth curve: nothing here has corners, because a corner asks you to stop and start again rather than to keep flowing, which is a different skill from the one the rest of the game is teaching. The shapes open up as your book fills — the gentle ones early, the busiest only once you have a real collection behind you.

    The ring you are following is drawn as wide as the margin you are allowed, so there is no hidden tolerance to learn — if your finger is on the pale road near the dot, you are scoring. That last part matters: you are judged on being on the road around the dot, not pinned to the exact spot it occupies this instant. A hand follows a moving thing a fraction of a second behind — that is simply what hands do — and being asked to sit precisely on it would mean only somebody who could see the future ever caught anything. A third of a second of lag costs you nothing; three quarters of a second is not keeping up. The dot and its halo go green while you are on it and red while you are not, the part you have already covered fills in behind you, and a bar along the top shows how you are doing against the line you need. The two rounds are averaged, not multiplied: a fumbled first half is something the second half can still rescue.

    Miss badly enough and it gets away — and it is still there on the grass afterwards. Losing one you can see is a miss; deleting it would be a punishment, and this is meant to be the gentlest thing in the village.

    And you can just ask what something is. Tap any bug — no catcher, no glass, no Gather — and a small card tells you what it is and whether it is in your book. That is all: looking at something across a field tells you its name and nothing else. Its line, and where it stands in your hundred and one, are what catching buys. Once a kind is in the book its line shows on a tap too, since by then you have been told it and it is written down anyway. Tapping a bug can never steal a tap meant for the tree it is sitting on.

    Then the card, and then it goes home. A catch stops everything and shows you what you have: drawn, numbered, named, with a line about itself and where it stands in your hundred and one — the same card the anglers already get. Close it and the catcher walks it back to the Bug Catcher's House, and the village hears what became of it — taken somewhere to be looked at properly, measured, written up, and let go. There are several ways it gets told, because it happens every catch and one sentence said a hundred times stops being read. Before the house is built they go to the town centre instead, where half the village has a look before it is released. No bug is ever worth a resource: the trade pays in knowing things. Nothing in that book is a trophy on a pin. It is a record of what has been seen, which is why the kind stays in the book and the creature goes back on the grass.
  • The Bronze Age wants a bit of everything now, in Peaceful. It used to ask only for knowledge and food, both of which come to you where you stand. It now wants wood, food, stone, gold, iron and knowledge — everything but the moonstone. Stone and gold are the two you have to go out and find, and iron asks for a little more than the stone alone brings with it, so you end up mining deeper than you meant to. The step out of the Wandering Age is untouched, and so is the Iron Age. The timed difficulties keep the old price: they are races
  • Peaceful gives up a fifth less of everything. Every resource now yields 20% less than it did — and for the first time that includes gold, iron and knowledge, which were exempt. They are still the least slowed of the seven, deliberately: gold has no seam to work at scale and the Iron Age hangs off it, so slowing it as hard as timber would push that age out of step with the rest rather than along with them
  • A trade is a person now, not a building. Twice a season, something turns up in the dark of the woods at the edge of your village — and the village smells it before it sees it. Warm bread on the air with nobody baking. A hammer going out in the trees when every hammer is accounted for. The woods humming out of season. Send somebody to look, and they carry home a loaf of wild grain, an old marked tool, a moonlit mushroom.

    Whoever carries it back may raise that trade's building — only them, and only one of each, ever. Raising it spends them: they take up the trade for life, earn a name for it, and leave your hands for good. The village is a pair of hands short and has a baker instead.

    Nothing conjures a worker out of thin air any more. A cottage with nobody in it simply stands there until you send a villager to take up the trade. Lose your herbalist and the hut is idle until somebody else steps in. The one who founded the village may find these things and put the buildings up, but never hold a trade — they have enough to do. And the Fisherman keeps his own way in, which was already exactly this shape
  • The Bakery is a cottage, not a hall. It sat on four tiles — as much ground as the Town Centre's neighbours — for one villager and an oven, and towered over the gardener's and herbalist's places beside it. One tile now, like the rest of them
  • Group 2 stops looking permanently selected, and is called by name. The founder's slot was lit gold from the first minute of every game, because the only marked state in the row was "there is somebody in this group" — and group 2 always has somebody. The bar now has three states instead of two: empty, in use, and the one you actually have in hand. Only the last of those catches the eye. And when the game tells you whose slot it is, it uses their name — "Group 2 is always Halvdan's", not "Halvdan the First's"
  • Fixed: the founder could be walked out of their own group. Group 2 is meant to be theirs permanently, and giving the slot to somebody else was already refused — but Ungroup emptied it in one tap, and so did joining any other group, and nothing ever put them back. Slot 2 was then empty for the rest of the match. Both doors are shut: Ungroup leaves them alone, and joining another group takes everyone selected except them
  • The book is a hundred now. Twenty-five more, spread across every part of it: six more of the common run, a fifth day fish to each season, a fifth pool fish to each season, three more of the deep-water things — and, at the end of the book, the moonstone fish. The Moonfin has been the only one of its kind for a long time; #93 to #100 are the rest of its family, all of them pale as the stone and all of them at the glowing pool after dark. Two of them are the scarcest things in the whole book. They get their own place in what the pool gives up, rather than being mixed in with the ordinary night catch — without that, better than a third of everything landed at the pool was a moonstone fish, which is no way to treat a rarity
  • Fixed: Harvest Home had stopped happening altogether. The autumn festival was set for the eighth day of the season — which was fine when a season was ten days long, and impossible from the moment they were shortened to seven. It has quietly not happened since. It is on day five now, properly late in the autumn, and all four of the year's festivals arrive again
  • Fixed: shoals had crowded together out in the water. When they were told to sit in open water rather than on the shoreline, the rule that keeps them spread out got spent first — so a stretch of water without much open middle packed its shoals almost on top of each other. The typical gap between the two closest shoals on a map had halved. They are spread out again, at a small cost: a few more sit near the bank than at the strictest setting, though still far fewer than before any of this
  • "An Eel", not "A Eel". Eight of the fifty-five fish start with a vowel
  • Fixed: the baker, the gardener and the rest pacing at their own front door. They walk to a working spot set at a fixed distance from their building — five past the right-hand wall, one below the bottom — and once anything is built next door that spot is inside somebody else's wall. It can never be reached, so they walked at it until a ninety-second timer let them go. In a tightly built village the baker's own spot was inside something in six seeds out of six, and the worst spells of walking on the spot ran 85 to 90 seconds, two thirds of a day, right beside their own door. Now they walk to reachable ground beside the spot instead, and any errand that has gained nothing for eight seconds is given up so they can find something else to do. Worst spell measured after: nine seconds. The same fix covers the farmhands, the beekeeper, the caretaker and the villagers out for a wander, who all shared the same five copies of the same walk
  • A new T button, just above Pause: what has been said. The message bar shows one line at a time and the next thing that happens writes over it, so a line could be half-read and then gone for good. Press T and the last two days of it comes back — scroll it, or close it with the ×. Grouped under the day it was said on, newest first. The village's own moments — an occasion, a discovery, somebody earning a name — are marked and read brighter than the ordinary running commentary, but the commentary is all there too, because the line you lost is just as likely to have been one of those
  • The peddler no longer sets up shop on your town centre. His rates used to appear among the town centre's own buttons whenever he was in the village — a second, different set of trades sitting where the building's upgrades go, with none of the Trading Post's context. Trading is the Trading Post's job. He still arrives, still gets his word on the way in and out, and still walks through the village; he is somebody passing through now rather than a shop
  • The village says when the Fisherman's House can be built. The fifth fish your fisherman lands now brings word that the house is theirs to put up — who they are, and to select them and open Build. The button has always appeared at exactly that moment, but only while that one villager is selected, and nothing announced it, so it was possible to fish for a season and never learn the house existed. Said once, on the fifth fish, and not at all if a Fisherman's House is already standing
  • One Kennels, one dog — and a Kennels now costs real money. It used to hand over the whole pack of four, so there was never a reason to build a second one. Four dogs is four Kennels now, and the price has gone up to 150 wood, 110 food and 30 gold. A dog is worth having, so it should be a decision rather than a box you tick once
  • Fixed: the grey bands running up either side of a pitched roof. Every building casts a shadow on the ground, and that shadow was a plain rectangle the size of its footprint — but a footprint is wider than a roof anywhere above the eaves, so its square corners stuck out either side of the slope as two hard grey stripes. It is loudest in winter, where bright snow turns the same shading into an obvious step with a straight edge belonging to nothing in the picture. The shadow is now a soft oval, the same shape the villagers have always cast, and it fades with the dark like theirs so it no longer sits as a stain over ground a brazier has lit
  • The town centre has taken its flag down. The little team-coloured pennant on a pole at the very peak is gone. Its roof is a tall clean pitch with a crossed ridge pole at the top, and the flag was one thing too many exactly where the eye goes first. The other grand buildings keep theirs
  • The dusk wind-down is gone — villagers set off home the moment night falls. They used to stand about for up to eight seconds first, "just finishing up", staggered so dusk arrived softly rather than all at once. In play it simply read as the village freezing at nightfall, and it measured as the single biggest slice of all the standing-about anyone does at night. Between this and the town-centre fix below, the time a villager spends stood still between dusk and bed is down by a third
  • Fixed: villagers standing about half the night instead of going to bed. When a few of them stop at the town centre for a last word before turning in, the gathering waited until every guest had reached their exact spot — but the walk gives up a little short of it, so one villager blocked by a corner or a barrow could never be counted as arrived, and the whole group stood there until a thirty-second backstop ran out. With the chat on top of it that was most of a night stood still. Now anybody who has stopped getting closer counts as arrived, and the backstop is twelve seconds rather than thirty. Also: the gathering can no longer take the whole village, which is what happened in a young settlement of five — everyone walked to the town centre and stood there, which looked exactly like the village freezing at nightfall
  • You can send somebody to go and play with a dog. Pick a villager, tap Gather, and tap a dog instead of a tree. They will walk over and make a fuss of it — a pat, and a game with the ball if the dog has one about. Works on all of them: the village dogs, and Gumby and Floyd too. Nothing in the menus mentions it and nothing ever will. Dogs already wandered up to people on their own and got made a fuss of; this is the same thing, asked for rather than waited on. Making a fuss of the same dog over and over is free and always welcome, but only the first one in a while leaves anybody walking taller
  • Fixed: if your fisherman died, nobody could ever take up the rod again. The post was held by a flag that was set once and never cleared, so losing them to a raid or a wolf meant the Fisherman's House quietly became unbuildable for the rest of the match — with nothing on screen to say why. Now the game simply asks whether anyone still holds the post, so it falls vacant the moment they do, and the next villager to sit down and play takes it up, with a name and an epithet of their own. Still only ever one fisherman at a time. The village is told when the post falls empty. Saves that already got stuck this way mend themselves on loading
  • Closing a catch card hands you straight back to the ordinary panel. It used to open a second screen of its own — "Rod's ready – go again?" with its own Play and Stop. Now that the ordinary panel carries Gather, Play and Stop itself, that was a second copy of a choice already on screen, asked somewhere else. One panel, one set of buttons, always in the same place. The rod still comes up out of the water ready to go, and they wait on you rather than quietly fishing on while you decide
  • Fixed: pressing Play often did nothing at all. A villager who reached a shoal started fishing on their own straight away, and that cycles the rod through cast, wait and reel — but Play can only start from the waiting bob. So the button was flickering between live and greyed about once a second, and since the panel only redraws a few times a second, the button you tapped was frequently already out of date. Measured: Play was live in only 15% of frames, flipping 19 times in 20 seconds. Now a villager arriving at the water waits with the line in, and does not fish until you choose Gather or Play — which holds the rod still and keeps the button honest. It is live 97.5% of the time
  • Sending somebody to the water gives you three buttons and no others. Tap a villager, tap Gather, tap the shoal — and the panel becomes Gather, Play, Stop. Move, Attack, Build and the rest are gone, because none of them means anything for somebody who is out fishing. Gather is lit, because it is what they are already doing: a villager at a shoal brings food in on their own and the game is optional on top. Play is the game. Stop calls them off and hands the ordinary panel straight back. The three appear the moment you tap the water rather than when they finally arrive — Play simply waits, greyed, until the line is actually in
  • Every village starts within reach of water, with one shoal already placed near the town, and the town centre itself can no longer be put on the water. All of this is meant to be available from the first morning of a Peaceful game rather than unlocked into
The fisherman, and his house
  • Whoever fishes first becomes the fisherman. They take a nickname built off their own — Fishman Joe — and the clothes to go with it, and they keep both for the rest of the village's life. It is first come, first served: nobody is exempt and nobody is chosen
  • He is 10% quicker on his feet than anyone else, which is the reason to send him rather than whoever happens to be standing nearest. And the Fisherman's House can only be built by him
  • The house is a boathouse. Same ground as an ordinary house — it takes no more room. A tarred roof rather than thatch, and instead of a door there is a boat bay: an arch with water standing in it and the nose of a boat just inside. Life ring on one side, netting on the other, anchor leaning by the opening
Elsewhere
  • The army does not sleep indoors any more. The wounded still take themselves off to their own quarters to mend, exactly as before. Everyone at full health now stays out all night — no bed, no barracks, no doorstep — which is what an army standing over a village ought to look like, and it means a night raid meets soldiers who are awake rather than soldiers who are in bed. This was supposed to be true already: the rule was written when the wounded got their quarters, and only ever covered the barracks, so the beds quietly went on taking everybody. Costs them nothing to be out, and nobody is pulled off a post by it — sentries stay in their towers and the watch still changes at dusk and dawn
  • Seasons are seven days rather than ten. Everything seasonal — the fish, the weather, what is growing — comes round noticeably sooner
  • Fixed a crash that could kill the picture outright. A tumbleweed was being handed to the code that draws the village dogs, which went looking for a coat colour on it, found nothing, and took the entire frame down with it — the game carried on underneath, invisibly. Roughly one match in ten. The suite now reads the drawing code itself and fails if two different things are ever given the same number again
Weather you can work through
  • You can keep people out in it now, and it costs. Heavy rain, a blizzard and a thunderstorm all send the village's optional outdoor life indoors — the doorstep scenes, the wanderers, the folk out for a stroll. Work was always exempt on purpose: a crew you have ordered to a woodpile stays on the woodpile, because that is your call and not the sky's. What was missing was the price. Anybody left out in it is now slowly soaked through: their health drains where you can see it, and the bar comes up so you watch it happening rather than finding out later
  • It never kills. It floors at a tenth of their health and stops dead there — ten minutes in a downpour leaves somebody miserable and standing. That is the whole difference between this and being dragged out of bed at night, which is a punishment that escalates toward death. This is a price for a decision you are allowed to make
  • And they dry out. Get them under cover, or wait for it to pass, and they come back to themselves. A cost you can never recover from would be a different game. Somebody already walking home is spared — there is no sense punishing a villager for doing the very thing you want
  • Asked about at the same time: villagers going in during heavy rain and never coming back out. Run properly for the first time and it does not happen — they do return. What makes it look permanent is how sparse doorstep life is by design: a scene needs the better part of a minute of cooldown and then a roll to appear at all, so after a long spell the doorsteps can stay bare for minutes together
Put right
  • Frogs, chickens, tumbleweeds and rabbit warrens have never once been drawn. All four worked out where they were on the screen and then drew there while the canvas was still set up for the world, so every coordinate was applied twice and they landed thousands of pixels off the edge of the map. They have been hopping, pecking, rolling and sitting there in perfect health, invisibly, for their whole lives. A sweep of every creature the game draws found all four; the other fourteen were fine
  • Nobody is sent to stand in the lake any more. When the village gathers at the hearth for a last word before bed, everyone is given a spot on a ring around the town centre — and the ring was taken entirely on trust. It cleared the building's own walls and then never once looked at what was actually underfoot, so a town with water at its elbow sent somebody to stand in it, where they can be walked at for ever and never arrive. It checks the ground now
The bugs were buried all winter
  • Every insect on the map vanished for the whole of winter. The drawing refused to show any of them unless something was still in bloom — and once winter properly settles, nothing is. The book has eleven winter species in it, among them a Snow Flea whose own note reads "black specks on white, and they move, which is how you know": a creature that could never once be seen, let alone caught, in the only season it exists. Which bugs belong out at a given time was already decided properly, one bug at a time; the blanket seasonal gate on top of it was simply wrong
  • And the flowering rule now names the two that do live off flowers rather than listing the exceptions. It was written the other way round and had missed the grasshoppers — so even with the season gate lifted, a Snow Flea would still have been hidden by a rule about blossom
Gumby and Floyd
  • They stop walking into buildings. Both picked where to wander next with a single roll and set off regardless of what was there, so about one target in thirty-five sat inside a wall, a house or the water — and they re-pick every few seconds all visit. The only thing that ever noticed was the stuck-watchdog, after they had walked into it and stopped. They now check the ground before they set off, which is what the village's own dogs have always done
  • And you can have a proper game with them. Send somebody to play with one and they got a pat and nothing else, while any kennels dog gives you a whole game of fetch — so making a fuss of the two rarest dogs in the game did less than making a fuss of an ordinary one. The fuss now turns into the same game: the ball goes down where you are standing, they bounce round it inviting you, and they take it back with them when they have had enough
The bugs are alive now, not stickers
  • Most of them had no movement of their own at all. Eight of the twelve bodies — the grasshopper, ladybird, beetle, spider, snail, worm, firefly and mayfly — never once consulted the clock, so however well they were drawn they were a still picture being slid across the grass. Each has a small life of its own now, and its own private clock, so no two in a group are ever in step
  • A beetle walks on alternate tripods, which is how a beetle actually walks — faster while it is going somewhere, and reduced to a slow fidget when it has stopped, because a beetle stood still is never entirely still. A spider's eight legs pick up and put down in a ripple, and go on testing the ground even at rest. A snail's foot ripples along its length, which is the whole of how a snail moves, and its two eye stalks sway independently. A worm sends a bend travelling down its body and gathers up behind it. A ladybird steps on diagonal pairs — it is the one thing out there that only ever walks, so still feet made it a bead on a string. A grasshopper works its cocked back leg between springs, because one sat waiting is winding up, and its antennae never stop
  • And the walk runs off the walking, not off a timer. The first pass swung the legs on a clock, which meant a bug that had stopped was still pedalling and a slow one was running on the spot — it read as a shake rather than a step, and was reported as exactly that. A leg cycle is now driven by how far the creature has actually moved, so it cannot out-run its own body: stand still and the legs stop, crawl and they turn over slowly, scuttle and they hurry. Measured standing perfectly still, a ladybird now shifts one pixel a frame and a beetle two, against two hundred and three hundred and seventy when walking
  • The mayfly's hover has been halved as well. It is older than any of this and not one of the new idles, but measured against everything else it was far and away the most restless thing on the map — the whole body swinging nearly its own height, over and over. It still hangs and bobs over the water, just less like it is being shaken
  • All of it deliberately tiny. At this size a large motion just reads as a flicker; the point is only that something is moving
A field is sown, comes up, and is cut — over days
  • Crops now start as seed in the ground. There was a real growth clock and the drawing already read it, but the earliest stage was "tiny shoots", so a newly sown field and a picked-over one looked the same. A field just put in is turned drills with the seed lying in them, nothing above ground, and the first green breaks the surface right at the end of that stage so it grows into the seedlings rather than cutting to them
  • And the cycle actually repeats. This was the real gap: nothing ever set the growth clock back to nought except the turn of a season. So a field harvested flat and reseeded on the second day of summer stood there in full ear again the same afternoon, and the whole seed-to-harvest story only ever played out once a season instead of every time the field was worked. Sowing a field now puts it back to seed, wherever the sowing came from — your own Replenish, the crew drawing on a banked reseed, or the other side doing the same — and it comes up again over the following days
  • Three separate places refill a field, and they had already drifted apart once before. They all go through one function now, so they cannot disagree again
Goblin camps watch their own gate
  • A level-three camp builds one lookout tower and it is meant to stand over the gateway — the one way in. It was only ever tried at two exact tiles, and when both were unusable (water, a tree, a stake already there) it quietly fell back to a random spot behind the camp, leaving the entrance watched by nothing. Measured: better than one camp in four. It tries properly now, and all fifteen camps measured put a lookout on their gate
You could not see the bugs, and here is why
  • They were all real, all drawn, and all somewhere else. Reported as simply not being able to see them, so it was measured rather than guessed. Around fifty insects were scattered evenly across an eighty-four by eighty-four map while you live inside about ten tiles of your hall — so at any zoom close enough to actually look at one, the count on screen was zero. Not few. Zero, at every zoom above a wide shot, and only a handful anywhere in the widest view
  • But not so many that the village is crawling. Gathering them near you made them findable and immediately made the place busy — seven insects in one small view, on top of all the other wildlife. Concentrating them was right; keeping the whole map's headcount as well was not, because all of it now stood in your ten tiles. There are a bit over half as many, which measured across eight maps takes what is on screen at an ordinary zoom from about seven down to three — and still puts eleven of the twelve different bodies out there, so the book can still be finished
  • Insects settle near the village now. Not the population — the number of them, how they are topped up, how they churn and the cap on them are all measured and completely untouched, so the book still fills at the pace it was tuned to. Only where they choose to be, which is also the truer picture: things with wings gather where the flowers, the crops and the water are, and that is your village. Measured across six maps afterwards: eight to twelve in view where there were none, and two to four even when zoomed right in
  • Every grasshopper was the same grasshopper. The body colour was written into the drawing and never once read the species' own, so the Field Grasshopper, the Meadow Grasshopper and the Wood Cricket all drew as one identical green speck — three separate entries in your book that could not be told apart in the world. They wear their own colours now
  • And the three faintest things out there have been lifted off the ground. Measured against bare earth, a worm shifted a pixel by 110 where a butterfly manages 425 — a dull brown line on brown soil with nothing behind it. The worm, the grasshopper and the spider now have the dark underside and ground contact that the ladybird and the beetle always had. Same insects, same size in the world; you can just find them
The magnifying glass is on the doorstep now
  • You could not find it, and that was fair enough. It was dropped six to thirteen tiles out from the hall and required to be lying under trees, which meant sending somebody wandering into the woods on the off-chance with nothing telling them where to look. It is two or three tiles from your town centre now — measured across twenty-four maps, never further than three and a half
  • And something finally says it is there. Nothing announced it at all: it was put on the map on the first morning and left, so the only way to learn the bug catcher existed was to stumble over it.
