The village now notices something in the grass catching the light, once, a few seconds into the first morning — late enough that the line does not land under the opening card and get closed along with it
  • And it looks like a magnifying glass now. Every trade find on the map is drawn as the same tied bundle — deliberately, because you are not meant to know what it is until somebody carries it home. The glass is the exception: it is the one every village starts with, and the one you are actively being told to go and pick up, so a wrapped parcel told you nothing. It lies in the grass as what it is — brass rim, a pale lens you can see the grass through, a glint, and a wooden handle running off to one side, the same glass the catcher ends up holding. Tipped over at an angle, because a circle sat flat on the ground reads as a coin, and sized to sit in the grass rather than dominate it
  • A building site no longer sits on a dark oval. Every building casts a soft elliptical shadow, which is right for a finished one — the ellipse exists so the footprint's square corners cannot poke out either side of a pitched roof, which they used to, as two hard grey bands running up the slope. But a half-built plot has no roof for them to poke out of, so all the ellipse did there was lie on the grass as a large dark oval with nothing standing on it. A site gets a rectangle now, squared off to its own footprint, which is also what a building site actually is: ground pegged out
  • And the founder may not pick it up. Nor any other trade find. Picking the glass up is not an errand you send somebody on — it makes them the bug catcher, for good — so handing it to the one who founded your village spends the single person you cannot spare on the one job that never gives them back. Tap it with them and the village says so. Anybody else may go
  • The trees are still preferred but no longer required. A hall standing on open ground used to fail every one of its four hundred attempts to place the thing and quietly end up with no glass at all — a whole trade missing from that match, with no message about it. Every one of twenty-four maps gets one now
Somebody at the edge of the village, waiting to be spoken to
  • A wayfarer stops at your boundary now and then, and only the founder will do. Not a trader, not a beggar — somebody who has walked a long way on purpose and wants to know whether this village is worth stopping at. They stand there until dusk and then they are gone, and there is never more than one of them at a time. Send anybody else and they will not speak; it has to be the one who founded the place, which is the only errand in the game that person alone can run
  • They ask you one question about your own village. How many souls are here. Which season it is. What the founder is called. Which of these buildings you have actually got standing. The wrong answers are the believable ones — a count a little off, a season either side, a building you could plausibly have raised — so it is a question about whether you have been paying attention rather than a riddle. The question goes up when the founder is standing there, not the moment you tap, so you are never answering for somebody still halfway across the village
  • Get it right and they stay, and they are genuinely better than the villager next to them. Four of them exist and each is good at one thing: a drover who moves half again as fast, a smith who hits far harder, a drifter who is close to twice as hard to kill, and a forager who brings back appreciably more. Each turns up once in the life of a village and never again
  • Get it wrong and they hear you out, shake their head and walk on. No penalty beyond the obvious one: the person you did not get. That wayfarer is spent, and the other three can still be met
  • Deliberately rare. Measured over twenty full matches, one turns up in roughly one match in six — often enough to be a thing that happens to you, rare enough that you do not plan around it
  • And the founder can talk to anybody on the road, not only the rare ones. An ordinary traveller stopping by could not be spoken to at all — the tap only ever looked for the four. Any traveller passing through can be talked round now, and they join as an ordinary villager: another pair of hands, no mark and no knack. Arriving better than the people you already have stays the wayfarer's alone, or the word stops meaning anything. Not everybody, mind — a peddler has a cart and their own trades to make, a thief has their own business with you, and the Ashkin's envoy already belongs to somebody else
You can get closer
  • The camera zooms in about a quarter further than it did. For the bugs, mostly: they are the smallest things in the game by a distance and the whole trade is about looking closely at one, which at the old limit meant squinting at something a few pixels across. A meadow grasshopper is a green insect on green grass — it is drawn, it is just very well hidden, and now you can actually get near enough to tell. Zooming out is untouched: pulling right back to see the whole map is worth keeping exactly as it was
The hens are something you keep now
  • Chickens are the town centre's first upgrade. They used to simply be there from the moment the hall went up. Keeping birds is a thing a village works out how to do, so it costs food and a little knowledge and it waits for the second age. A village you have been playing for months keeps the ones it already had — it is not charged for them twice
  • And a hen does more than peck. That was the entire repertoire, so five birds in a yard read as five copies of one bird. There are six things she might be doing now, each a real pose rather than a different speed of the same one: pecking still, raking the ground backwards with one foot and looking up to see what came loose, preening with her head turned right back into her wing, standing with her head up turning slowly at nothing, a short burst of flapping that lifts her off the ground, and sitting down in the dirt to have a dust bath with her legs tucked away underneath her. Pecking is still much the commonest, because that is what a chicken mostly does
  • They go inside when the weather turns, rather than blinking out of existence. Foul weather used to simply delete every bird where it stood and conjure a fresh lot out of nowhere when it passed. They walk to the hall door now and go in, and they come back out after — and nothing startles them on the way, because being spooked used to override the walk indoors and strand them in the rain
  • Sometimes one, some, or all of them go and have a look at the farm. A proper outing: they walk over, potter about outside it for a while, and come back. The yard's leash lets go of a bird that is visiting, and the stay only starts counting once she has actually arrived — timing it from the moment she set off meant any farm more than a few tiles away was never reached at all
  • And they no longer get pinned against the corner of a building. A hen walking into a wall had her destination reset to her own feet, every frame, which stopped her for good and also hid her from the very check meant to free her. She slides along the wall now, and a separate check watches a whole second of net movement — the old per-frame version scored her as fine while she jittered on the spot going nowhere — and sends her somewhere else if she is getting nowhere. A hen who cannot reach the farm at all gives the outing up and goes home
  • In winter they barely come out. Two birds rather than five, and a lot longer between them — a yard with a hen or two picking about in the frost rather than the summer crowd. Not none at all: an empty yard for a whole season reads as a broken feature rather than as the cold. A full summer yard thins out when the season turns instead of standing about in it
  • One more, found on the way: only somebody actually walking scatters them. A villager standing still is furniture as far as a hen is concerned. Measured before this: in a settled village somebody is stood near the hall essentially always, so every bird was permanently mid-flee and not one of them ever settled long enough to do anything at all
Patch 21.20
Four things to find, and none of them found the same way
  • Five one-time finds already existed and every one of them worked the same way: something glows, you walk a villager to it. Four more now, and the point of them is that no two are found alike. Each unlocks a building nothing else unlocks, and each can only ever happen once in a village
  • The mill wheel. After a storm has blown itself out, something heavy grounds itself in the shallows — a wheel, with spokes, off a mill that is not coming for it. Bring it in and you can raise a Watermill, which grinds, so the same fields feed further than they did. Its top rung grinds harder still
  • The arrowheads. Nobody goes looking for these. Somebody working an ordinary stone vein eventually breaks into a whole cache of worked flint — hundreds of them, knapped by somebody who knew exactly what they were doing. That unlocks a Fletcher's Hut, and every archer you train from then on reaches further
  • The wolf pup. Only after your village has come through a night raid, and only in the dark: something is making a noise in the trees that is far too small to be what made it. Take it in — nobody has the heart to argue — and you can build Kennels, which train hounds, a fast unit that is on your side of the fence from here on. And a hound that has been sent at something it cannot possibly reach gives up and comes home, rather than standing there about it until the end of the match
  • The standing stone. This one is a scout's find and only a scout's: one sent a long way out from the village comes on a stone standing on end, taller than a person, carved all over with marks nobody here can read. Turns out the marks are weather. Somebody stood there a very long time ago and wrote down what the sky did, and it still holds. Raise a Weather Stone of your own and the almanac stops being a two-day proposition
  • The wounded mend in their own quarters. A soldier carrying a wound now spends the night in the building that trained them — the swordsman in the barracks, the archer at the range, the rider in the stable — and comes out at first light in far better shape than they went in. Measured: about half a soldier's health over one night. Only the wounded go in. Anyone at full health has no reason to be in there and stays out, so the village never looks emptied of its garrison at dusk. No orders, no clicking: they take themselves off, and they don't dawdle on the way. If their own building has been lost there is nowhere to mend and they stay out — they will not bunk in somebody else's
  • The mist stopped looking like ellipses lying on the grass. The ground mist is drawn as drifting oval banks, and each one faded out along a straight run to nothing — which leaves an edge the eye picks up, so instead of air you saw a shape with a rim. It is thinner now (barely half as heavy at its thickest) and fades away in four gentle steps that ease off towards the rim, so there is no stretch of constant slope for an edge to sit on. Same mist, same size, same slow roll — you just can't point at where one ends any more
  • "Then…" is gone, and the builders just get on with it. The toggle you had to arm before giving a busy unit its next order has been taken out. The one job it was really doing — line up a few buildings and walk away — a builder already does by itself: finish a site and they look round for the next unfinished one and start on it, without being told and without a mode to switch on first. One builder will see three sites through on its own and go back to gathering afterwards. A button you have to remember to press is a worse answer than the villagers simply doing the sensible thing
  • Moonpetals are worth going out for again. Measured, one was opening on the grass on one night in three — far too often for the best of the three night finds, and it had turned into something you expected rather than something you were pleased to see. It is one night in eight now. The owl feather has been held exactly where it already was: it is rolled after the petal, so it only ever saw the nights the petal turned down, and making the petal rarer would otherwise have quietly promoted the feather from one night in six to one in four without anyone asking for it
  • The moon on the almanac ring, at last. Reported twice and "fixed" once by making it bigger and paler-blue, which changed nothing, because the crescent was never drawing at all. It is built from two arcs sharing their two ends, and the inner arc's radius was smaller than the gap it had to span — so it was quietly stretched until it fitted, became the same curve as the outer one, and left a shape with no width whatsoever. The sun was always fine; the moon was an empty outline every night since the ring went in. It now rides the bottom half from dusk round to dawn the way it was always meant to
  • The doorstep parent is an actual adult now. Somebody who comes out to meet a soldier home at dusk used to be drawn as the same half-height figure used for children playing in the yard — the original ask was specific, that it look and move like an ordinary villager, different clothes only. It does now, at full size, in the household's own colours, off the real villager body. Fixing it turned up two real bugs that had made the old figure invisible in practice: its own clock started at zero, so it despawned on the very first frame every single time, and it never once picked a walk target because the timer that would have started it moving was left unset
  • The village's working people get a life. Six people walk out of six buildings, do one thing and walk back — the caretaker, the baker, the beekeeper, the gardener, the geologist and the granary's farmhand — and every one of them then stood dead still at their own door for the three quarters of a minute in between. The gap is right; nothing happening during it was not. Now they potter a few aimless steps and back; they go and work at their own trade's thing outside the door — the baker at his oven, the caretaker at his seed sacks, the gardener at her bed, the geologist at his spoil heap, the beekeeper at the skeps; and they go over and talk to each other, or to any villager standing about, both of them turned to face one another for as long as it lasts. All of it is dropped the instant a real errand comes up: the job always wins
  • The Geologist stops making ore altogether. He opened new veins at random, and when that was fixed he deepened existing ones instead — better, but still quietly manufacturing ore the map never had. Neither survives. He works a spent seam back open and does nothing else, at 12% of the seam a visit rather than 40%, and never past what that ground actually held. When everything within reach is full he simply has nothing to dig today. The Deep Seam now keeps every seam already in reach of the cottage rather than only ones he opened, so buying it works on the ground you already have
  • The Gardener plants outside the village, not through it. He was planting anywhere within reach, so over a long game a wood grew up through the middle of the streets — trees against doorways, trees in the square. He now keeps clear of the buildings and works the edge, so the village holds its shape and the woods thicken around it
  • Both cottages are day work, and the night shift is somebody's job. Their second rung no longer hands out a night shift the way every other building's does. It builds a bed — and you may then post a villager there with Garrison, who works the beds or the seams through the night while the gardener or the geologist sleeps. Take them out again and the cottage goes back to keeping daylight hours. The panel shows you who is on tonight
  • Buildings look like their trades. They read far too alike — the same box under the same roof, and you had to find the little icon to know what you were looking at. Four of them now say what they are from across the village. The Bakery has a red pantile roof and a brick oven standing outside its door, mouth glowing, chimney smoking — and that oven is the thing the baker actually walks out to. The Caretaker's Cottage has a dull tin roof over its green boards, with seed sacks slumped by the step. The Gardener's Cottage has a turf roof and a bed outside that follows the year: bare canes in winter, shoots in spring, flowers in summer, something heavy and orange in autumn. And the Geologist's Cottage rises out of the ground — banked round with spoil and loose stone, with the propped mouth of his own working cut into it
  • The pup in the woods comes every year now. It used to be a single roll after a night raid: miss it and there was never another one, ever. Instead you now hear it before you see it — something crying out in the dark, far too small to be whatever woke you — and that happens once a year, certainly, and never twice in the same year. Send somebody out to fetch it. And this is the part that matters: if whoever went for it does not come back, neither does the pup, and you wait until next year to hear another. It is worth thinking about who you send
  • The dogs prance, and now and then one turns up with a ball. A dog that has been made a fuss of will sometimes drop its ball at that person's feet, put its front end right down in a play bow and spring — and then skip a foot or two one way, spring back the other, and keep switching sides, the way one does when it wants you to join in. A ball is not something they carry about all day: one turns up every couple of days, gets played with, and is gone again, so a dog with a ball in its mouth is worth noticing. And they have three markings now on top of the four coats, which are unchanged: plain keeps the saddle patch, piebald breaks it up with a white chest, blaze and socks, and ticked speckles the flank. Four dogs are now very unlikely to be the same animal twice
  • The Kennels becomes a village building, with dogs in it. It has moved out of Military and into Village, where it belongs — most of what a kennel actually puts into a village is dogs wandering about in it. It still trains hounds, because that is what finding the wolf pup buys and moving the building must not make that find pay nothing. What is new is four dogs, and they are not scenery parked by a wall: they trot off somewhere, stop dead to sniff at the ground, sit down, break into a run for no reason whatever, and go over to see anybody standing about. Each is on its own clock, so four dogs never do the same thing at once. One body in four coats — sandy, liver, wheaten and blue-grey, and deliberately never black, because black is Gumby and Floyd and they are somebody's own dogs. And a villager who stops to make a fuss of one goes back to work about a tenth quicker for the next half minute. You cannot order it: you get it when your people and the dogs happen to meet
  • You can tell the Gardener and the Geologist apart. They were the same figure in the same clothes, and the only way to know which was which was to watch where they walked. The gardener is in green now, under a broad straw hat, and carries a spade while there is a job on. The geologist wears a lamp strapped to his brow — lit, after dark — and pushes a barrow out to the seam, coming back with something in it. Neither carries a tool while they are stood at home, so the village looks like it is working rather than like it owns two costumes
  • And neither of them stands still any more. Both used to stand dead still at their own door for the three quarters of a minute between errands, in plain sight. The gap is right — the work is meant to be occasional — but nothing happening during it was not. They potter now: a few steps to somewhere near the cottage, a pause, a few steps back, never further than a stride or two from the door and dropped the instant there is a real job on
  • The Geologist stops inventing ore. Once nothing near his cottage was short, he would wander off and open a brand new vein somewhere at random, and over a long game that scattered ore across the whole village. He works the ground you already have instead: he goes out to the best seam in reach and makes it bigger — more in it now, and more it can ever hold. The map keeps the shape it was dealt, the ore near a cottage quietly becomes worth more than the ore anywhere else, and a seam that has been worked to its limit is simply left alone. He will still open new ground in one case only: a cottage built where there is no ore within reach at all
  • The Gardener and the Geologist get the top of their ladders. Both cottages shipped with two rungs and a gap where the third should be. The gardener's is The Orchard: everything he plants from then on is grafted stock, and felling one of those gives you a crop as well as the timber — for as long as the tree stands, whatever happens to the cottage afterwards. The geologist's is The Deep Seam: a vein his cottage opened is timbered and worked properly, and wins a little of itself back every night — the one thing in the game that comes back from empty, everything else being recovery rather than resurrection. Both cottages also move down to the Stone Age, because a three-rung ladder needs three ages to climb through and a Bronze Age building has only two left above it
  • Walls go up in runs. A wall is the one building you never want just one of, and putting up a line of twelve meant going through pick, tap, confirm twelve times. Now you choose a run — 1, 2, 5 or 10 — and which way it lies, and the whole line is staked out in one go. The ghost shows you the run before you commit to it, green where each length will stand and red where it will not, so a rock or the water's edge in the middle of your fence is something you see rather than discover. Whatever fits goes up and the panel tells you how much of it will (“8 of the 10 will fit”), the cost quoted is the whole line's, and the length and direction you chose are remembered for the next stretch
  • Moonstone trees move. They were fixed at the start of the match — the same one in fifty trees, glowing every night for ever — so you learned where your two were in the first ten minutes and never looked again. That is scenery you happen to own, not something to go out for. A different handful is touched each dusk now and lets go at dawn: they are ordinary trees by daylight, they are somewhere else tomorrow night, and felling one by day is felling an ordinary tree exactly as before. The rival's woods light up too. Same idea the moonstone veins have always worked on
  • The players' bells were round their ankles. The travelling troupe wear bells — it is most of what makes them players rather than three strangers in odd colours. They were being drawn an inch off the ground, so what you actually saw was three gold discs rolling along at each performer's feet. They hang from the belt now, on their own threads, each swinging on its own as they walk
  • No more fog circles. The mist under the village, the cloud shadows crossing the ground and the clouds themselves were all built the same way — a scatter of big soft ellipses drifting about. However gently one of those is faded at the rim it still has a middle and an outside, so what you actually saw was a field of grey discs lying on the grass rather than weather. All three are flat now: mist is one even translucent sheet across the whole view, cloud shade is one even dimming of the ground, and the drifting clouds are gone entirely, leaving only the slight paleness an overcast puts on everything. Each still comes and goes on its own timing and still thickens with the season and the weather — there is simply no shape anywhere in any of them to catch your eye. Measured, the mist lifts the ground about a quarter of the way towards white: plainly there, still perfectly see-through
  • Footpaths stop being made of squares. Tracks worn into the ground were painted one tile at a time, as a filled square per tile — so a village anybody had actually walked around was covered in a grid of hard-edged blocks, and every path visibly stepped from tile to tile instead of running. The wear is now drawn as one soft mask blended up to size, the same way the fog already was: a track narrows, widens and fades out exactly where the traffic does, with no straight edge anywhere in it. Paved roads keep their joints — those are meant to look laid, and only show on a well-worn Bronze Age road when you are zoomed right in
  • The Noticeboard keeps the village's record. It had two pages already — a list of rare things you happened to see, and the diary of what actually happened. What it never had was the third kind: things you set out to do. Thirty-two deeds now, in four groups — settling, the village, the wider world, and trials — each with a name and a line of its own when you earn it, and the counted ones show you how far along you are rather than just staying dark. Earning one is said out loud and written into the diary in its own hand. The page leads with the deeds now instead of a wall of question marks, and the sightings list has become a section further down. Per village, not a career record: this is what this village has done, and a village months old picks up every deed it has already earned the moment it loads
  • The almanac reads further ahead. With a Weather Stone standing, Today and Tomorrow are joined by the days after — up to five out, once the stone is fully raised. It will not pretend to know more than it does: past the end of the season the game has actually settled the weather for, the far cells say Too far to say rather than repeating one guess three days running
Patch 21.19
Three buildings moved down an age
  • The Caretaker's Cottage is a Bronze Age building now instead of Iron. It is the same kind of thing as the Gardener's and the Geologist's cottages — one person who walks out, does a job, walks back — and it sat two ages later than both of them for no reason anybody had written down. Measured, neither of the caretaker's days ever came up in a full peaceful game, because Iron is the better part of an hour away
  • The Trading Post comes to Bronze too. Market day — every fifth day, better rates — is built entirely around it, and at Iron the whole feature was dead for the first hour of a village
  • The Moonstone Cottage joins the Moonstone Manor in Bronze. The Manor is the far bigger and far more expensive building and was already there; the small cottage that houses two more night workers being a whole age later was backwards
  • All three gain a new first upgrade to fill the age they have moved into, so each now has a proper two-step ladder with the night shift on the second rung, the same as everything else
Every ladder's second rung is now a night shift
  • Upgrade a building twice and it keeps working after dark. One meaning, one rung, right across the table — you learn it once and it is then true of everything. A farm, lumber camp or mine on its second rung has a crew that is simply not sent home at dusk; they work it by lamplight. A Barracks, Range, Stable, Town Centre or Dock goes on training and building right through the night instead of stopping at dark. And the Caretaker, Gardener and Geologist — who never slept anyway — come round a second time after dark instead, two rounds a night rather than one
  • It is bought, not given: a night-shift crew gets just as tired as any other night work, and is owed its night wages at dawn. Round the clock costs you food and tired villagers. It is also not the same as dragging somebody out of bed — that still takes health off them permanently and still kills them in two nights. A shift is a rota
  • Nothing works any less well than it did. The rung only ever adds hours
Fixed
  • “They is being mauled” on the first night, and “Bryony finally head home to rest” — two messages whose wording only worked when the villager had no name, or only when they did
Nights
  • The will-o'-the-wisp. A pale light comes up out on the wet ground that, at any distance, looks exactly like moonstone — the same cool pool, thrown the same way. Send someone after it and it moves off, keeping ahead of them, drawing them further and further out. Most of them are lying and leave your villager a long walk home in the dark. Some are not, and there is something real at the end of it. You cannot tell which this one is, and that is the whole of it
  • The quiet night. A night with nothing in it at all — no visitors, nothing at the fences, nobody hurt — and the whole village wakes properly rested and says so
  • Night wages. Whoever you kept working through the dark gets fed first at dawn, and it costs a little food. Pay it and nobody begrudges it. Have nothing to give them and they go back out on an empty stomach, which costs you rather more than the breakfast would have
  • The lunar eclipse. One night a year the moon goes out entirely. Every moonstone thing stops glowing, the dome can chart nothing, and it is darker than the village has any use for. The almanac names the date a week ahead, so it is the one night you can prepare against rather than simply receive
  • The lights are worth something now. The aurora has always been in the game and has always been scenery. While it is up, every moonstone glow reaches twice as far and veins show from twice the distance — so the lights are a night to be out in, not just a night to look at
  • A star that lands. Not the shooting star you catch — something comes down hard in the night and is still there in the morning: a scorched crater with sky-iron in it, warm for a while, and workable for two days before it goes dull and crumbling. The only thing in the game whose consequence you walk out to at first light
  • Charting the constellations. On a clear night the Observatory charts one named constellation — the Plough, the Hare, the Forge, the Net, twelve in all. Each is charted once ever, each is worth a little of something forever after, and the Noticeboard keeps the list of which you have. Clear nights stop being an income line and become a collection with an end
  • The charcoal burn. A new Charcoal Kiln. Villagers stack it with wood through the day; when it is full it lights itself at dusk; and then somebody has to sit up with it. Draw it at dawn and you have charcoal, which makes the Blacksmith and the Armoury better than wood ever could — and it stacks, burn after burn. Leave it to itself and it burns through to ash and you lose the wood and the night both. That is rather the point: a night job you cannot fail is a timer
  • The beacon chain. A new Beacon: a basket of fire on a frame, unlit. Light one after dark and every beacon within sight of it answers, and the one beyond that — a line of them showing you the country all night. They eat wood the whole time they burn and they go out at dawn, so where you put them is the whole game
  • Wassailing the orchard. On a midwinter night, if you have a gardener and trees to go out to, the village takes a bowl out to them, shouts at them, bangs on pans and pours the last of the cider over the roots. The woods come back faster for the whole year after. It is a real custom with a real purpose, and it has never yet failed to work
  • The vigil. The night after somebody you knew by name is killed, the ones who knew them keep a light at the town centre until dawn, and their name goes in the diary. It costs nothing and pays nothing, and it is meant to stay that way
  • Moths at the lamp. On warm nights they gather at braziers and lit windows — a crowd at a brazier, three at a cottage. None at all in the cold or the rain
The day gets an event pool of its own
  • Something can happen in the daytime now. The night has had a proper event pool for a long while — forty-odd things that can turn up, weighted, never the same one twice running. The day had nothing of the kind: a handful of scattered one-offs which, once found, never happened again, so a village a month old had run out of daylight surprises entirely. The day now runs the same machinery the night does
  • The village keeps a diary. Every occasion writes a dated line in the village's own words, and you can read the whole thing back on the Noticeboard. Lines used to scroll past in four seconds and be gone; a village played over months now has a history rather than just a save file
  • The year's firsts. First blossom, first swallow, first frost, first snow — noticed once each, every year
  • A lost traveller. Somebody wanders in plainly turned around. Tap one of your villagers onto them to feed them and set them right, and a bundle with no name on it turns up at the town centre the next morning. Ignore them and they drift off no better off. And once in a while they were not lost at all, and go straight to the Ashkin with everything they counted
  • Bees, properly. Swarms are a summer thing and not every summer — roughly one in three, so a village can wait years for one. It is announced by degrees: the bees are noticed in the clover, then heard from the doorstep, then seen going up in knots over the hedge, and the day after that the swarm settles. Those lines only ever appear in a summer that really has one, so they are worth reading
  • Send anyone out to it and they get stung getting it into the skep, then carry it home — it is a box of bees, not a load of wood, and nothing can be done with it until it is back in the village. Whoever brought the first one in is the beekeeper from then on, veil and smock and all
  • Every swarm carried home lets you build one Beehive, about the size of a house. A keeper works it and carries honey round the village — to the fields, the houses, the bakery — and the whole village is a little the better for having bees at all. It upgrades over the ages: more skeps, then a proper bee house, then an apiary the village is known for. A hard winter can empty a skep, but it leaves the building standing, waiting for the next swarm
  • The strange mood. A villager with a name stops work and will not say why. They take over a workshop and wait on particular materials — some of which you may not have. Find them within three days and they come out carrying something nobody has seen the like of, with a name on it, and they are the best in the village at their trade ever after. Fail them and they go back to work, and they are not the same as they were
  • Travelling players. A troupe comes up the road in motley and bells and sets up in front of the town centre. Everyone stops to watch, and afterwards the whole village works quicker for the rest of the day. They were also, historically, reckoned to be thieves — so once in a while something is missing when they go
  • Hue and cry. The stores are opened in the night and at dawn there is somebody on the open ground, moving quickly, with your goods. The whole village is entitled to drop what it is doing and go after them. Run them down and everything comes back with a good deal that was never yours to begin with; let them over the hill and it is gone
  • The peddler at the gate. One trader, one mule, three offers, gone by dark, and plainly worse rates than the night market. Something to turn down
  • A wedding. Two of the regulars — the people the village actually knows by sight — marry at the town centre. Everyone turns out, no work of consequence gets done, and afterwards there is a household at the end of the row that was not there last week, with somebody new in it
  • The village's own people get days of their own. The caretaker, the baker, the beekeeper, the gardener and the geologist each walked out, did one thing on a loop, and walked back. Now: the caretaker turns up coin under a floor, or is out before anyone else patching whatever is most broken, unasked. The baker makes a loaf the length of a table on a festival or market day and the whole village gets a piece — or runs the flour bins down to the boards and stands in the doorway with his arms folded until the stores come up. The beekeeper takes the season's honey off the hives, and once the bees find your fields every crop sets heavier from then on — though a hard winter can take a hive. The gardener grafts a cutting that becomes a real fruit tree over the following days, or brings something out of the beds nobody can name. And the geologist reads a seam far deeper than anyone thought, or reads the ground and tells you there will be moonstone up tonight — and there is, because the promise is kept rather than merely made
  • The spring, and the dry well. Somebody strikes water: a well built on that spot costs nothing at all, this season only. Or a summer turns hard and hot, the stream goes to stones, and with no well in the village everyone works at half strength until there is one. Build it and the relief is immediate, and said out loud
Patch 21.18
A few small signs of life
  • Night raids now scale with how far along whoever they're aimed at is — one creature at a time in the Stone Age, two in the Bronze Age, and a real pack of three by the Iron Age, sometimes two different kinds together rather than always the same one multiplied. Raiding the rival scales to their own progress too, not yours
  • Soldiers go home at night. One standing about inside your own village at dusk — not garrisoned, not under orders, not out on the map somewhere — walks to a house and turns in until dawn, the same as everybody else. Somebody who lives there comes out to the door to meet them, and it is the same household every time
  • A soldier below half health doesn't dawdle at dusk the way the rest do — they set off for a bed at once
  • Two veterans (the ones carrying the pale streak in the helm crest, earned by surviving three fights) sit up at the hearth on a Nightcap evening, closer to the fire than anyone, and stay on a while after the rest have gone in. The streak still carries no bonus of any kind and never will
  • A clear night is worth something now. The Observatory does almost nothing by day. Under an open sky after dark it earns several times what it used to, more again on a full moon, and under rain, snow or fog it earns nothing at all. It tells you which sort of night it is at nightfall, if you own one
  • Market day, every fifth day. The carts come in and the Trading Post's scales are kinder — about a third better on every trade, on top of the post's own upgrades and on top of a merchant's good night if the two happen to land together. Fixed to the calendar rather than rolled, so you can hold a surplus back for it
  • The almanac says what's next. A third column beside Today and Tomorrow, naming the soonest thing that is genuinely on the calendar — market day, the season turning, or the moon coming full — and how many days off it is. Not a weather forecast: the game only plans one season of weather ahead and this column won't pretend otherwise
  • Four days that belong to the year. One day in each season now arrives on a fixed date, is announced days ahead, and does one thing only it does. Blossom Day in spring seeds every field at once. The Long Table in summer feeds the whole village — everybody carries the day's edge, not only the army. Harvest Home in autumn counts in the year's return, paid on the fields you actually built. And Midwinter is the long night itself and the fire that answers it, rather than a fifth occasion beside it. All four fill the streets for the day
  • The boat that goes out at night. Everything else goes in at dusk. One thing goes out: if you own a Dock and a fishing boat is idle when the light goes, it takes a lantern out onto the deep water and works until dawn. From the shore all you see all night is the light out there. It comes back low in the water — several times a day's fishing — but the boat is gone for the whole night and nothing is guarding it, and rough weather brings it home early with only what it has caught so far. Give the boat any order at all and it stays in
  • The long night. One night in the middle of every winter the light goes half again as early and dawn stays exactly where it was, so midwinter really is the shortest working day of the year. Everything nocturnal doubles with it — two things out in the dark instead of one, moonstone twice as readily. The almanac warns you a week ahead, in its own column and in the day's line, because the whole point is having time to decide what to get done before the light goes
  • Three things that only open after dark. The night had exactly one thing worth going out for, and it was moonstone. Now: a moonpetal opens out on the grass at full dark — food, and whoever picks it and everyone near them comes back rested. An owl feather comes down through the trees late on — knowledge, a little gold, and for a moment you see the country round it as the bird did. And dawn dew lies on the fields in the hour before the sun is properly up — food, and it waters the nearest farm. One at a time, all of them gone if you don't go out for them, and the dew needs fields to lie on
  • The watch changes. A garrisoned sentry used to be posted for ever — put someone in a tower on day three and they were still in it a month later. Twice a day now, at dusk and at first light, whoever has been up there longest comes down and somebody else walks up to take over. At dusk the relief walks out as everybody else walks in. It only ever swaps when there is somebody free to swap with, so a lone sentry is never left with an empty tower, and the tower itself is unchanged — same garrison, same defence
  • Children keep hours. They come out after the middle of the day and are called in as the light starts to turn, before anybody else goes anywhere. The animals keep no hours whatever — a dog is out when it wants to be, which is rather the point of doing this to one of them and not the other
  • Regulars. Everyone you saw out and about used to be a stranger — a new name, new clothes and a new errand every single time. Two or three of them are the same person now: the same face, the same errand, the same spot, day after day, until the village remarks on it. They are this village's regulars, kept with the save and retired quietly if their house comes down
  • Rain sends people indoors. When the weather properly arrives, everything optional stops — nobody out for a walk, nobody skipping stones, no children on doorsteps — and it all starts again when it eases. The street emptying is now the first sign the weather has landed. Work is untouched: a crew you have ordered to a woodpile stays on the woodpile, because that is your call and not the sky's. Fog is exempt, since fog is exactly the weather worth being out in
  • The middle of the day. Around noon the work slackens off for a few minutes — tools down, people turning to whoever is nearest — and then it picks up again. It comes over the village as a ripple rather than everyone stopping at once. They come back with a short second wind that pays for about what the break cost, so it is something the village does rather than something it loses
  • Nobody works a night for free. A villager you keep gathering after dark is worn down by it, and is still trudging through the first half of the following morning — a bed is what mends it, not sunrise. Soldiers standing a watch are unaffected, as they always were
Fixed
  • The almanac's Today and Tomorrow forecast had been quietly wrong since seasons went to ten days: from the third day of a season onwards, both cells were reading the next season's weather
  • The forecast also read “A squall gets up expected” and “A blizzard sweeps in expected” — the panel was wrapping its own words round a phrase that already had a verb in it. Each kind of weather now has a short name for the panel and keeps its full line for the moment it actually arrives
  • The three things that only open after dark were nearly invisible at full dark — measured, a moonpetal lifted the ground it stood on by five points of brightness and the dawn dew by none at all, because a glow drawn with the world keeps about a fifth of its contrast once night falls over it. All three now light the ground properly, the way a moonstone vein does. They are the things you are being asked to go out into the dark and find
Patch 21.17
Fixed
  • Continuing a saved village after actually closing and reopening the game (rather than just staying on the same page) could throw the moment anything with grass on it came into view, and every frame after it. A cache of baked grass images was being written into the save as a set of hollow shells that only look real once the browser has properly forgotten them — harmless in testing, but not in an actual saved game reopened later. Villages saved before this fix are repaired automatically the next time they load
  • The Captain's Station had no upgrade of its own, the one building that had slipped through when every other building was given one. It now has a Muster Ground rung, training the Captain a little faster
  • Wandering pilgrims could get wedged against a building or a shoreline and stay there for the rest of their visit. Their own "am I making progress" check was judged frame to frame, which a pilgrim nudged back and forth at a corner could pass on plenty of individual frames while going nowhere overall - the same blind spot villagers themselves had before they were given a check judged over a few seconds instead of one frame at a time. Pilgrims now use that same steadier check
  • Double-tapping the town icon to bring the camera home did nothing during the Wandering Age, right when a lone founder is most likely to need it - it was quietly requiring the town centre to be fully built, not just standing
  • A lumberjack's own flannel shirt sat right on top of the team-colour sash that keeps everyone else's side readable at a glance - hard to tell your own woodcutters from the rival's. They now carry a second, plainer band of team colour at the belt, clear of the check pattern
A few small signs of life
  • A soldier fighting badly hurt now shows it in how they move — a slight limp, one arm held a little in — rather than only in a health bar
  • A villager with genuinely nothing on — not working, not walking anywhere, not sat down — sways gently now and again instead of standing dead still
  • A couple who spent the day together get one warm light at their own door as they turn in for the night
  • The Noticeboard occasionally reports on a couple out and about instead of the day's usual history fact
  • A sleeping villager's dream can now, about half the time, carry a soft hint of tomorrow's weather
  • A fighter right at death's door trembles a little rather than standing perfectly steady through the last of it
  • An earned name keeps meaning something afterwards — Stonehand mines a touch faster, Timberarm cuts a touch faster, and the same for the field-earned name at their own farm
  • A household that lived through a bad night stays wary of the woods for a while — still out and about, just not for an afternoon reading under a tree
  • A night event that hasn't turned up in a long while is now a little more likely to be the one that does, rather than a long game leaning on the same handful of common ones forever
  • The Noticeboard can now report on the village's own prosperity — a running read of population, buildings, named villagers and discoveries, not a target to hit, just something to feel good about
  • A new "Then…" order button: arm it and the next order given to a unit that's already busy is remembered rather than replacing what they're doing, and taken up the moment that job actually finishes — queue "build this, then gather" in two taps instead of waiting for the first to be done
  • The baker's whites no longer darken with the cold like everyone else's clothes — he's meant to be recognisable at a glance year-round, and winter was quietly working against that
  • The baker doesn't just stand at his own door on a quiet day — when there's no round to run he ducks inside for a spell, or carries a loaf over to somebody's house, so he's doing something even between rounds
  • The Caretaker's Cottage now banks up to three replenishes in one visit instead of one — a busy farm could run dry before he walked all the way back round to it again
  • A Granary now sends out its own farmhand, walking out to one of your farms and back — a sight, not a mechanic, so a farm reads as somewhere someone actually goes
  • The baker has a third thing to do on a quiet day now, besides ducking inside or visiting a house — pottering about right outside his own oven
  • A soldier who has come through enough fighting now carries a small permanent mark of it — a pale streak through their helm's crest, never a stat change, so an army isn't purely disposable identical bodies
  • A nightcap at the hearth: most nights now, a handful of villagers pause at the town centre for a few minutes before bed for one last wordless chat — a light, common cousin of the rare night the elder tells a story by the fire
  • Dusk no longer sends the whole village home on the exact same frame — everyone gets a few seconds of "just finishing up" first, staggered per villager, so the village winds down rather than snapping over like a light switch
  • Night fishing now has a moment worth reacting to — watch for the float jerking hard instead of its usual steady bob, and tap your angler quickly for a bonus catch on top of the ordinary moonlit haul. Miss it and it costs nothing
  • The Night Market is no longer a total ambush — if a cart is coming tonight, the almanac says so a day ahead, so trading with it (and the raid risk that comes with buying) is a decision you can actually plan for
  • Once you've met the hermit, autumn brings a small ask of your own — a little wood before winter, given by tapping a carrying villager onto the hermit itself. Miss the season and there's always next year
  • A storm passing, or rough weather clearing, can wash a shipwrecked chest up along the water's edge — a one-off find of gold and salvaged wood, worth a look before someone else's tide takes it back
  • A message in a bottle can wash up too, now and then — a mysterious note with a genuine playing tip rolled up inside. Leave it too long and it washes back out, but another can always turn up another night
  • A villager claims a house of their own well before dusk now, rather than having nowhere to call home until night sends them looking, and one with truly nothing to do will sometimes wander a few tiles on their own rather than standing dead still all day
  • Repairing one of the five ancient ruins is a real decision now, not a free find — once fully mended it waits for you to choose and pay for how to finish it: the safe, familiar way, or a costlier, more ambitious one with a bigger payoff
  • A repaired ruin now carries a small plaque set into its own wall — a quiet mark that this one is found, finished, and someone chose how
  • A new Iron Age building, the Sunstone Cairn: it produces nothing, trains nothing and defends nothing, and costs more than anything else you can build — a wonder for a village with nothing left to spend on, and nowhere to put it but pride
  • A rare night can now be a proper meteor shower too, not only a lantern festival — half the village comes out to watch, on top of the ordinary run of falling-star wishes
  • A thriving village now genuinely feels busier, not just older — how many off-duty villagers you'll ever see out and about at once grows with the village's own prosperity, not a flat number every village was stuck with regardless of size
  • A new Bronze Age order, Fortify: send a villager to a wall, tower or your fortress and pay a little wood and stone for a temporary shield — real extra protection that soaks up damage before your walls take it, and runs out on its own after a while if it's never needed
  • A new Village Chronicle on the start menu — a short memory of your last ten matches, win or lose: who founded it, how far it got, and how it ended. Separate from your one saved village, so nothing about it is ever at risk
  • The date at the bottom of the screen now traces the day itself — a thin ring behind it, with the sun riding the top half while it's up and the moon taking over the bottom half once it isn't, so you can see roughly how much of the day or night has gone at a glance
  • Two new Bronze Age buildings: the Gardener's Cottage sends someone out to tend a struggling tree or plant a seedling where the ground allows; the Geologist's Cottage does the same for gold and stone veins, opening a thin new seam rather than a full deposit. Either takes a couple of days to grow in properly. Both work for free, quietly keeping the map from ever being picked completely bare
  • A rare tree in the woods carries moonstone - it looks like any other by day, but glows after dark, and felling one by moonlight brings home wood and moonstone both
  • Some trees come into cherry blossom for the length of spring, a splash of pink scattered through the ordinary green
Patch 21.16
The Captain
  • A new hero-tier unit for the Iron Age: the Captain, trained at a new Captain's Station. Taller than anyone else in your army, bare-headed on purpose, carrying a kite shield and a blade that always carries a faint moonstone-blue light — a light-blue hue by day, a proper glow after dark, lighting the ground around him the way a torch would without carrying one
  • Only one can ever be in service at a time — training a second is refused, whether it would come from the same station or another one, until the first falls
  • His attack cycles through three distinct swings — from the left, from the right, then an overhead slam that throws whoever he's fighting off their feet. He plants his feet and trades blows rather than circling his target the way the rest of the army does
  • The Captain's Station itself is sized like the Caretaker's Cottage, built in ash-grey stone rather than the usual timber, with a pair of spare blades crossed by the door

Stats and training cost are still a placeholder — the finished unit is meant to cost a real share of every resource, moonstone included. The knock-people-into-the-air slam is in; a leadership buff for nearby soldiers is not built yet.

Patch 21.15
Fixed
  • Some Ashkin villages could get permanently stuck before ever reaching the Stone Age — a small enough economy meant nobody was ever put to gathering wood specifically, so the settlement sat on plenty of everything else and never quite the timber the next step needed. They now always keep enough hands free early on to actually get past it, whichever way they otherwise like to play
  • A small-economy Ashkin could field a real army on Peaceful but never build a single wall or tower, since that only used to kick in with a bigger village than that kind of side ever keeps. Now it doesn't take nearly as much
Patch 21.14
Floyd
  • Gumby has company — Floyd, a second little dog, smaller again and after something different: where Gumby raids a farm, Floyd makes off with a sock from the nearest house. Tap either one to see who they are
Peaceful keeps growing
  • The Ashkin on Peaceful now keep building the whole match through — more villagers, more soldiers, a wall or two, a watchtower, an armoury — instead of stalling out partway. They still never march on you first: leave them be and they simply become a steadily bigger, better-defended village, so the longer a match runs the more there eventually is to reckon with if you do pick the fight
Fixed
  • Gumby could spawn standing on ground he could not actually stand on, and would then never move again for the rest of the match — about one visit in four. He (and Floyd) now check the ground is clear before trotting in
  • On Peaceful, the Ashkin's army could sit stuck at the same size for a real stretch of the match while resources piled up waiting on the next age — and on some maps, holding every resource back at once meant they never quite banked enough food to age up at all, however much everything else piled up
Patch 21.13
Ground, sky, and the light between them
  • The wind travels now. It was one number that every blade, tree and field obeyed at the same instant. A gust is a band that crosses the country instead: the grass goes over in a ripple, the trees on the far side lean a beat later, the crops bend as it reaches them, and it passes on
  • Every bird goes up before the rain. A quarter of a minute before the first drop the roofs empty, a flock lifts out of the fields, and they are gone — the same warning the light gives, in the language birds use. Once per spell
  • Once a season, the air fills with something. The firefly swarm was the best small thing in the game and it only ever happened after dark — so now every season has its own, by day, and you will see it at least once in each: Bloomtide beetles in spring, every one a different pastel; dragonflies in summer that hang still and are then twenty feet away; gossamer on the wind in autumn; and diamond dust in winter, crystals of ice hanging in the cold and flashing in the sun. None of them does anything. That is the point of them
  • The sea has depth to it now — deeper water out from the shore and lighter shallows against it, swell running at two different scales, and torn scraps of foam at the edge instead of the row of perfect circles that used to sit there
  • Reeds at the water's edge, which lay over when a squall comes across the water. And at dusk and dawn a fish rises on still water and leaves a ring spreading behind it
  • Grass, everywhere the ground is grass. It leans on the same wind that moves everything else, and a few blades cross the boots of whoever is standing in it — they bend aside as somebody walks through and spring back behind them. Nothing is ever hidden in it
  • Lean in and there is more there. Close to, a finer bed appears that does not exist further out: taller wisps, and seed heads once you are right in. Pull back and the grass steps aside for the big picture
  • The water moves at every edge. A swell runs ALONG the coast rather than pulsing everywhere at once, foam breaks at the top of each run, and the wet sand it leaves behind lags a moment behind the water — which is what makes the sea look like it is going out rather than just shrinking. Rough weather runs it up harder
  • There are clouds now, not just their shadows. Pull out and you can see them crossing above the valley, with their shade crawling below and behind them — the gap between the two is the height. Come in close and they fade to almost nothing, as a cloud should when you are looking at somebody's boots
  • It goes grey before it rains. The light starts draining out of the day about half a minute before the first drop and keeps going until it breaks. The almanac tells you in words; this tells you in the language weather actually uses. And the ground is never quite the same shade twice
Day one
  • A new match now opens with three lines and an X: you have woken alone, gather wood to repair your town, stay safe at night and attack if you have to. The world waits until you close it. It also tells you the two ways back if you get lost — tap Idle to find your villager, double-tap the small town icon on the row of group numbers to get home. Loading a village you already have does not show it, you have read it
  • Your first villager carries a torch. They are the only villager who ever does. You begin with one person, on a map you have not walked, and a lone civilian carried no light at all — so the moment it got dark you lost sight of the only thing you had
  • Goblin camps get teeth from level two. A camp that has come back stronger fields archers and puts up lookouts — lashed poles with a hide platform, and they shoot. It also brings war brutes: half again the size of an ordinary goblin, that much harder to put down, with a ridge of a mohawk and a bone guard on the shoulder so you can see one coming. Their club comes round in an arc and catches whoever else is stood beside the one it swung at, so a line drawn up shoulder to shoulder in front of one is the wrong shape to fight it in
  • Their clubs are proper weapons now — dark wood against the skin rather than the same brown as the arm holding it, with small iron spikes set into the head. It is the only metal anywhere on a goblin, which is what makes the club look like something they made rather than a branch they found
  • The camp itself shows its level: a second rank of stakes, lashings in the tribe's own colour, and a rack of bones by the door from level three. None of it starts anything. You can walk right under a lookout and it will watch you go — and now you really can, because a sleeping camp used to kill anything that wandered within a few paces of it while insisting it had never noticed you
  • Villagers pick berries by hand. They had a felling axe out and were swinging it at the fruit — and at wheat fields, come to that. Now they reach into the bush, one hand in as the other comes out, turning to face whatever they are working. You can see a berry in the hand on the way back, and the basket they carry home holds the fruit in the colour it actually was when it was picked
  • The fruit ripens as the season runs. Each season walks its berries through three colours and the bushes shift between them, so a patch you gathered from at the start of autumn is a different colour by the end of it — green and hard, then blushing, then ripe in spring; scarlet, then damson, then sloe-dark in autumn. Every bush keeps its own clock, so the one in the sun ripens first
  • You hear the goblins before you see them. The first camp of a season announces itself in four steps as you close on it: chanting somewhere out in the dark at night, then voices arguing in a language of hard sounds, then a shout going up when they spot you, then war drums — and they still do not move. Walk away and the drums fall away behind you. By the time you have met them once, only the drums still play
  • The berry bushes are properly drawn now. They were one flat green ellipse with four red dots on it — and they are the first thing you ever walk up to. Now there are four different bushes, built in layers with a ragged leafy edge, and they turn with the year: rusty in autumn, in blossom with the fruit still green in spring, twigs under snow in winter. Five small matte berries when full, fewer as they are picked, so a bush that has been worked looks picked over rather than shrunk
  • Three berry bushes at your town, and only three. A start used to be ringed with twenty of them, which made the first half hour a walk between berries rather than a reason to build a farm. Three is about three hundred food: a second and third pair of hands, and a field to put them on. Wild berries out in the country are half as common as they were — worth sending a scout for, not enough to live on
Mist, and a foggy day
  • Mist now gathers in the low ground. It lies between the ground and the village — roofs, people and lamplight stand clear above it, and what it does is mute the ground it is lying on. It is thickest by the water, thin on open ground, and after dark you mostly see it where there is light to see it by
  • You will catch it at dusk, through the night, and at dawn, where it is heaviest. It comes up on its own and burns off slowly when the sun gets to it rather than blinking out. Nothing about it is still: every bank sways, rolls and swells on its own slow clock
  • “A foggy day” is now real weather, and the almanac will forecast it. A season that rolls weather may roll fog instead of its own rough spell — autumn is the foggy season, spring nearly as much, a summer fog is rare
  • It is the one weather that is not rough. Nothing is damaged, no brazier is blown out, and you can walk in it perfectly well. What a fog takes is your sight: you cannot see as far in it as in anything else, a blizzard included. The birds stay out too — it is only hazy, not foul
Something passing the camera
  • Once in a while something crosses right in front of you at night, far too big to be standing on the map — a moth in the warm half of the year, a bat in the cold. It is past in a second and a half. It did not fly across the village; it flew past you
  • By day, seeds, blossom, leaves or frost blow between you and the village, close to the lens and out of focus. They slide faster than the ground does when you move the camera, which is what makes them look near
  • Both are treats rather than furniture — about one match in four, like a sky full of stars
And a sky that stayed one evening
  • A starry sky now belongs to the night it turned up in. It used to hang over the morning if the night ended first, and weather could close in over the top of it. Either one puts it out now, easing away over a few seconds rather than vanishing between two frames
Patch 21.12
Villagers you actually know
  • A villager can earn a name. Most of your village never will — and that is the point. The handful who have one have it because of something they did, and the panel will tell you what
  • Four ways to earn it. Stand through the first night and live. Sit through three of the elder's stories. Work one job for a whole season without being shuffled off it. Or be picked out by the world itself — led away by a fox, sat at the hermit's fire, carrying a season's seed home
  • The name fits the deed: Bjorn Frostwake for standing through a winter night, Arne Timberarm for a season at the trees, Runa Foxfriend, Ylva the Well-Told. Your founder is the First
  • You are told the moment somebody earns one — an anonymous villager becoming a person in front of you is the whole point of it. The first deed is the one that names them; anything later is kept in their record but never renames somebody you already know
  • Tap one and the panel says who they are, how long they have been about and what they have done. And if somebody you know by name is killed, you are told which one
A world without dead ground
  • Map generation used to leave threads of land one tile wide winding through the water where a pond had cut through a coast. Nothing can be built on them — not even the smallest building — so they were dead ground that looked like somewhere you could settle. They are gone: any land that is not part of a solid two-by-two is taken back by the water, and the new shoreline gets its sand like any other
Goblins — Peaceful gets something to fight
  • Peaceful has an enemy now, and it is entirely up to you whether you ever meet it. Somewhere out in the unexplored country a goblin camp is pitched: a hide hut, a couple of shacks and five goblins hanging about. They will never come for you. You have to go and find them, and then you have to start it
  • Start it and you have started it properly. Hit one goblin, or one of their buildings, and the war drums go up and the whole camp comes for you until it is levelled. Everything of theirs has to go — every goblin and the hut — and clearing it pays 100 of every resource, carried home
  • They are tied to the seasons. A camp belongs to the season it turns up in, and there are four tribes: the same goblins, in four different skins and four different warpaints. Spring is sour green with a stripe up the face, summer tan with a red band across the eyes, autumn russet with claw-slashes, winter grey-blue with rings round the eyes like sockets
  • Beat one and next year that season comes back a level harder, up to level five. Levels show as an added colour on their belts, wrists and clubs — blue, black, silver, then gold — so a level four autumn goblin is plainly the same autumn tribe in better kit. Leave a camp alone and it strikes its tents when the season turns and comes back next year exactly as it was, so nothing is ever lost by walking away
  • The camp pitches somewhere new every year, always well away from both villages and always out in ground you have not walked. Torches burn either side of their hut and light the camp as far as your own hall lights yours — but a camp you have not found yet stays dark, so it never gives its own position away
  • The Ashkin have no quarrel with them and they have none with the Ashkin. This is your war, and only if you want one
  • Your Noticeboard keeps the tally — four seasons, five pips each, filled in as far as you have got, and what level is waiting for you next
The first night, and the one who started it all
  • Your very first villager has a name now, from the moment the match begins, and the panel says so: their name, and underneath it, that they founded your village. Months into a Peaceful village you can still tap them and see who the whole place grew out of. There are 168 names to draw on — Norse, Old English and Swedish — so you are not running a town of nine people all called Bjorn
  • The first night now comes for you every single time, not two starts in three, and what comes depends on the season you began in: a bramble beast in spring, a dust scorpion in summer, a night bear in autumn putting on weight before the cold, and the frost lynx in winter
  • And it will not fight itself. Your villager used to turn and defend themselves without being asked; they do not any more. Select them and send them at it, or they die — and with the town centre still a ruin, that is your run. You get a clear warning when it appears and one more nudge if you have not moved. It is the first thing the game actually asks you to do
  • Send them at it and they will win, but it is a real fight, not a formality — expect to come out of it at about a quarter health. Rest puts it right: they mend steadily once nothing is biting them, so surviving the night is not a wound you carry for the rest of the match
  • On Peaceful it can never take more than two thirds of them. The lesson still lands — something comes out of the dark, they are mauled, and it is plainly your job to do something about it — but a Peaceful village is never lost to it. Every other difficulty means it
The small hours
  • The night is not just a darker version of the day any more. There are small things about: moths that gather at your braziers, the odd drifting firefly, and spiders hanging on threads by the walls
  • Which of them are out depends on the season — moths and fireflies from spring, spiders arriving with the autumn. Winter is nearly empty, because nearly nothing flies in winter: a few spiders sheltering by the buildings and that is all. The quiet is the point
  • And rarely — about one night in six — a single glow bug, crawling low with a steady light of its own. It is meant to be a thing you notice and point at rather than scenery, so there is never a field of them. Each season has its own colour: new green in spring, warm gold through summer, an ember orange in autumn, and a cold pale blue in the snow — the only light out there on a winter night
  • They are gone by morning, the way they are gone when you go looking in the daylight. Every one of them has its own size, its own speed and its own wander, and there is a breeze that moves the lot of them together
  • The firefly swarm is untouched and still its own rare, announced occasion. This is the everyday texture underneath it
The baker's round
  • Somebody works at the Bakery now. During the day he comes out in his whites and his tall hat, with a basket of loaves in both arms, and walks to wherever your soldiers actually are — a barracks, a range, or a company camped out in the open. Bread handed round, empty basket, back to the oven. He does not go out after dark
  • He works out where the round is worth walking, rather than simply going to the nearest thing: he counts how many hungry soldiers each stop would actually reach and goes where the army is. Villagers get nothing — it is the soldiers' bread — and neither does the scout out exploring, or he would spend all day walking to one man
  • A loaf lasts a day. The Bakery's own bonus and its upgrades are still the full-time part and have not changed; this is on top, and it wears off by tomorrow morning. So there is a right moment to attack — catch your army just after the bread has gone round and they hit harder than they will in the morning
  • He is one of the same people as everyone else out there, drawn the same way, with his own face and height under the coat. He costs no population, cannot be selected or ordered, and nothing can hurt him
The old smith's own way
  • Repairing the Old Blacksmith used to hand you its ancient tempering free, the moment the last stone went in. It is the fourth and best level of armour in the game, so you buy it now — at that forge, and at no other forge anywhere. What finding the ruin gets you is the only place in the world that sells it
  • One purchase, all three armour lines at once, and it stacks on top of whatever ordinary tier each of them has separately reached. It wants the Iron Age and 140 iron and 120 gold — dearer than tier two, as the level above it should be
  • Before the Iron Age the forge names it and shows it greyed rather than hiding it. You went and found the thing; you should be able to see what it is for
The caretaker gets up and goes
  • The Caretaker's Cottage used to top up your farms by changing a number where nobody could see it. Now somebody actually lives there. They come out of the door, walk across the village to whichever field is lowest, spend a while sowing it, and walk home again
  • They look and move like everybody else out there, because they are drawn as one of them — their own face, their own height, their own clothes. They cost no population, cannot be selected or ordered, and nothing can hurt them. They are simply somebody doing a job
  • The wood is paid when they arrive, not when they set off. Spend your last log while they are still walking and they turn round and come home rather than sowing a field out of nothing. Knock the cottage down and its caretaker goes with it; build two and there are two of them
Every building can be improved
  • Every single building in the game now has an upgrade in every age it is able to stand in. Select one and its own next improvement is there in the panel, named, priced and with a line saying what it does. A farm, lumber camp, mine or house can be improved four times — the first of them while you are still a camp, before the Stone Age has been paid for. A Stone Age building has three, a Bronze Age one two, and an Iron Age building has its single one
  • They belong to the building, not to you. Four barracks are four separate ladders and four separate bills — the same way the gather research and the watchtower rebuild have always worked. And the work mends what it touches, so a damaged building comes out of an upgrade whole
  • Each one does something you can feel rather than a number going up: a Drill Yard turns recruits out faster, a Second Hearth makes room for another family, a Timber Chute sends the logs down to the camp on their own, Standing Stones give the village something to think about, Iron Battlements give a fortress the reach to use them. Nothing is filler
  • Several buildings that quietly did nothing at all now do something. The Shrine and the Noticeboard produce knowledge once they have been built up. The Trading Post finally earns its keep — your own scales, and a better rate on every trade you make. The Well waters a village that works better for it
  • The four that already had a research line — farm, lumber camp, mine and the Elder's Lodge — kept it, and gained the rungs below it. So does the brazier. Only ever one upgrade is offered at a time, so what you see is a single ladder that carries on all the way up rather than two competing buttons
  • The Ashkin buy them too, one at a time, and hold back what they owe on their own town centre before they spend on anything else
  • None of it is lost on an old village: anything saved before this simply starts at the bottom of its ladder with everything still to climb
The camp, and then the village
  • Getting the town centre standing no longer hands you the whole game at once. It makes you a camp: there is a bed, the hearth is lit, the wilds start taking an interest — and you may build a farm, a lumber camp, a mine and houses. That is what a camp does. Everything else waits
  • What ends the Wandering Age is upgrading the town centre, on the same button every other age-up has always used: 100 wood and 50 food, and your people enter the Stone Age with the rest of the build order open to them. Measured over a dozen matches, the camp lasts about three days — long enough to be a stage of the game rather than a loading screen
  • The almanac says Wandering Age for the whole of it, camp and all, and only turns over to Stone Age when you have actually paid for it
  • The Ashkin live under exactly the same rule, hold back exactly the same hundred wood, and cannot start on a barracks before you can
  • Villages already in progress are not sent back for any of this. Anything with a town centre standing is in the Stone Age on load and is not charged for it a second time — whether it was saved last week or an hour ago
Before the Stone Age
  • A match no longer opens with a working town and five pairs of hands. It opens in the Wandering Age: one villager, nothing whatever in the stores, and the town centre standing in ruins. There is no build menu and nobody to train — the only job in the world is to fetch the 70 wood the repair wants, and do it. Roughly a day's work
  • Wherever you start, the ground provides: berries within a few paces of the ruin — enough for a second pair of hands and a farm besides — and trees close enough to begin on straight away. Whether the opening is work or a search should not come down to the roll of a map
  • And while you are still out there, your people see further than they will once they are settled. One villager and no scout is little enough without searching blind as well
  • Get it standing and your people settle: the roof goes on, the hearth is lit, and the Stone Age begins. Only then do you find out what this particular ground was good for — the village's own small gift is held back until there is a village to give it to
  • Until the centre stands there is nowhere to sleep, and a night in the open tells. Anyone who spends it out there is dead on their feet by morning and works and walks at a fraction of their pace — nobody dies of it, but you will feel it. One night indoors puts it right, and once you are settled it stops being a worry at all
  • The Ashkin start exactly the same way and have to do the same work, so it is a race out of the rubble rather than a handicap. On a harder difficulty their ruin is further along than yours to begin with
  • Nothing in the dark will come for you while you are still in the ruins. With one pair of hands and no walls, a single hungry animal on the second night would not maim somebody — it would end the game outright, with nothing you could have done. The wilds notice you the moment the hearth is lit, and from then on the night is exactly as dangerous as it always was
  • Your first night is not always a quiet one. Two times in three something comes out of the dark for whoever is out there — a lynx in winter, a wolf otherwise. They will turn and fight it without being told to, they will come off much the worse for it, and it will break off and slink away rather than finish them. They mend by morning. The dark has things in it, and you want a roof: that is the whole lesson, and it costs you nothing but a fright
